title: Task Convergent Flow Matching for Generative Robotics
summary: Successful manipulation requires the manipulated objects to progress toward a desired task outcome. Generative policies can produce plausible robot motions without ensuring this progress, allowing successive action chunks to stall or undo earlier changes to the scene. We introduce a task-centric inference-time refinement framework for flow matching policies that evaluates candidate action chunks through parallel physics-based rollouts and searches for motions satisfying sufficient conditions for task convergence. Task-level performance funnels bound temporary regressions while requiring net progress over each chunk. We establish sufficient conditions under which repeated funnel satisfaction yields convergence throughout execution, and use interval-wise Lipschitz bounds to verify continuous-time funnel satisfaction from sampled rollouts. To accommodate contact-rich hybrid dynamics, we refine the flow's source seeds using derivative-free Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), constrained to radial quantile bands of the source distribution to help retain the learned motion prior. This formulation supports both Euclidean and pose-valued Riemannian Flow Matching (RMFM) policies. On PushT and three-cube stacking, refinement raises success from 31.3% to 88.5% and from 77.0% to 86.0%. On PushT, whose coverage score responds continuously to the motion of the block, a learned funnel lowers the average maximum loss of achieved progress by 19% relative to constraining the endpoint of each chunk alone, at a similar success rate. With the radial band, 11.3% of the executed motion windows are out of distribution, a rate within the range of held-out demonstrations, compared with 34.1% for an unconstrained search.

title: EvoSkill-S1: Evolving Reusable Skills with Genetic-Inspired Operators
summary: Reusable skills allow language-model agents to accumulate and reuse problem-solving experience. However, most existing methods improve a skill bank only indirectly through rollout-driven accumulation and heuristic reflection, often resulting in shallow and weakly controlled updates. We present EvoSkill-S1, an RL-driven framework that instead treats reusable skills themselves as the direct objects of evolution. Given hard-negative failures, EvoSkill-S1 selects parent skills and transforms them into candidate child skills through five genetic-inspired operators: revision, cross-revision, mutation, dual-reflection, and crossover. Downstream task rewards train the skill evolver to generate more effective child skills, while evaluator-guided write-back selectively retains beneficial updates. Complementary Skill Bank Fusion consolidates operator-specific banks to exploit their distinct recovery patterns, while a Procedural Skill Interface supports transfer to unseen problems. Across all reported math and code benchmarks, EvoSkill-S1 improves the corresponding initialized skill banks under both Qwen and GPT-family solvers, with relative gains of up to 12.39%. Compared with the strongest external baseline without direct skill evolution, the largest relative improvement reaches 20.39%.

title: DAQ: Decision-Aligned Post-Training Quantization for Spiking Transformers
summary: Spiking transformers combine attention-based representation learning with sparse spike communication, yet their weights and membrane variables still incur substantial storage and computation overhead. Post-training quantization (PTQ) offers a practical way to reduce these overheads, but preserving neuronal firing under weight and membrane quantization remains challenging. In this paper, we propose Decision-Aligned Post-Training Quantization (DAQ), a method that calibrates the quantizers to align neuronal firing decisions with those of a floating-point reference. We analyze how errors from these quantizers affect firing at decision boundaries and how they propagate over time steps in recurrent neurons. Based on this analysis, we formulate an objective that encourages quantized membrane variables to remain within the reference firing regions along the quantized model's own state trajectory. Experiments across multiple spiking transformer architectures on image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking demonstrate the effectiveness of DAQ with 4-bit weights and membrane variables. On FE108, DAQ achieves 58.8\% AUC and 90.9\% PR with SDTrack, while reducing energy by 66.2\%.

title: Right Diagnosis, Unsafe Route: Auditing Clinical AI Decision Trajectories and Corrective Oversight for Validity and Potential Harm
summary: A clinical AI system can reach a correct final diagnosis through intermediate decisions that could have harmed the patient, and can repair an error while introducing new risks. Most evaluations score final diagnoses; even stepwise benchmarks, which release a case's evidence over time, score whether systems reach the right diagnosis or gather the right information, not whether the decisions a patient passes through are safe. We make patient safety the target of stepwise evaluation. A trajectory audit replays real admissions checkpoint by checkpoint, lets each system decide with only the evidence released so far, and rates every test, treatment and disposition for its potential harm to the patient and, separately, for clinical validity, against the documented final diagnosis and physician-written disease rubrics yet on the evidence available when the decision was made. An LLM judge scores every decision, and a physician reference standard (triple annotation and senior adjudication of a stratified sample) calibrates the rates. An oversight audit branches each trajectory at its first actionable error and measures, on the same branches, whether corrective feedback repairs the error and whether it introduces new harm. Across 300 cases from a hospital cardiology cohort, MIMIC-IV and the public ASCENT benchmark, with up to seven AI systems per source, 55.2% of hospital trajectories reaching an acceptable final diagnosis passed through a decision with moderate or severe potential harm and 24.8% through a clinically unacceptable one; the harm rates were 76.2% on MIMIC-IV and 39.6% on ASCENT. Structured corrections resolved 73.6% of first errors versus 24.8% after bare rejection, yet new potentially unsafe decisions followed 30.2% of corrections versus 19.7% of rejections. A correct final diagnosis does not certify a safe trajectory, and a successful correction does not certify a safe recovery.

title: Python Code Generation for Isabelle/HOL
comments: 20 pages, 19 figures, 2 tables. Software artefact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24106993
summary: The Isabelle theorem prover provides an environment for formalising mathematics and reasoning about programs. To make verified implementations practically usable, its code generator translates functions expressed in the executable fragment of its logic into conventional programming languages. Its targets have traditionally been functional languages (Standard ML, OCaml, Haskell, and Scala), recently joined by Go. Python, which is becoming the dominant language of scientific computing, data science, and education, has remained out of reach. In this work, we close this gap with a Python backend for Isabelle's code generator. This generator enables verified algorithms to be used in Python applications, or to serve as verified references against which established Python libraries can be differentially tested, without leaving the Python ecosystem. We validate the backend on regression suites covering large parts of the HOL library and by testing six verified data structures and algorithms against established Python libraries. The generated code is slower than hand-written libraries, but well suited as a verified reference.

title: An Affordable Vibrotactile Surface for Tactile Figure Recognition: Exploration Strategies of Blind and Sighted Users
summary: Refreshable tactile displays can make graphics accessible to blind and low-vision people, but high-resolution actuator arrays remain expensive. We study whether a low-cost vibrotactile surface can convey simple figures, and how they are read. Nine participants (four blind; five sighted, tested blindfolded then open-eyed) identified seven figures by touch, with video and timing analysis of their exploration. Blind and blindfolded-sighted readers achieved comparable accuracy, but blind participants were about three times faster, using a continuous, rhythmic "gliding" strategy-reading through motion, whereas sighted participants searched in halting, pause-heavy passes; among the sighted, more pausing accompanied errors. Recognition failures were concentrated in specific figures (a diagonal was misread even with vision), locating the bottleneck in representation rather than resolution. We contribute an empirical characterization of tactile reading strategies and design implications for low-cost refreshable tactile displays and affordable tactile representation.

title: A Divergence-Free Finite Element Discretization of a Convection-Cooling Optimal Control Problem
summary: In this paper, we develop and analyze a finite element discretization for a bilinear optimal control problem governed by a stationary convection-diffusion equation, in which an incompressible velocity field acts as the control through the convective term. Continuous piecewise linear finite elements are employed to approximate the state and adjoint variables, while the Stokes-type optimality equation for the velocity control is discretized by a low-order, pointwise divergence-free ($P_1^c\oplus RT_0-P_0$) finite element. To accommodate the nonconforming velocity space, we construct a discrete cost functional by replacing the continuous $H^1$-seminorm regularization with a suitable discrete velocity bilinear form and derive the corresponding discrete first-order optimality system. Since the bilinear coupling between the velocity control and the state variable renders the underlying optimization problem nonconvex, we establish local strong convexity of the discrete reduced cost functional under a second-order sufficient optimality condition at an isolated strict local minimizer of the continuous problem. Furthermore, by exploiting a divergence-preserving interpolation operator, auxiliary state and adjoint error estimates, and a stability relation between the discrete reduced-gradient residual and the control error, we derive a priori error estimates for the state, adjoint state and velocity control. Numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the optimized incompressible velocity in redistributing the temperature field and to verify the predicted convergence rates.

title: Hardness and Inapproximability of the Covering Radius for LDPC Codes
summary: Given a binary parity-check matrix $H$ and an integer $r$, the covering-radius decision problem asks whether every attainable syndrome can be represented by an error vector of Hamming weight at most $r$. We study this problem for sparse parity-check matrices with bounded row and column weights. Using a bounded-occurrence quantified-SAT reduction, we prove that the problem is $Π_2^{\mathrm P}$-complete for matrices with maximum row and column weight three, and remains $Π_2^{\mathrm P}$-hard under a constant multiplicative gap. Starting from Vertex Cover on 3-regular graphs, we also obtain an explicit NP-hard approximation factor under the same weight constraints. We remark that weight three is the exact threshold for hardness: if either the maximum row weight or the maximum column weight is at most two, the covering radius can be computed in polynomial time.

title: Understanding Cross-Modal Inconsistency through Representation Subspaces in Omni Models
summary: Omni Models process audio, vision, and text within a unified language backbone, yet often produce different answers for semantically equivalent inputs across modalities. Existing representation-level analyses do not distinguish between information that predicts whether disagreement will occur and the representation whose perturbation affects the model's answer. In this paper, we estimate a low-dimensional Answer Subspace from answer-position representations and use it to separate answer-related components from the remaining representation. Across three Omni Models and two multimodal reasoning tasks, information predictive of cross-modal inconsistency lies mainly outside the Answer Subspace, concentrating in a reproducible two-dimensional representation that is not explained by a fixed modality offset. Matched interventions reveal distinct behavioral roles: perturbing the Answer Subspace substantially changes the model's predictions, whereas perturbing the disagreement representation, like a random subspace of the same dimensionality, leaves them almost unchanged. Our key finding is that cross-modal disagreement can be induced by misaligning modality-specific answer representations: perturbing the Answer Subspace for only one modality induces disagreement, whereas applying the same perturbation to both largely preserves agreement. Thus, the representation that predicts disagreement is distinct from the answer-level representation through which disagreement can be induced, showing that linear decodability does not imply behavioral efficacy.

title: What Do LLMs Use to Judge Synthesis Recipes? An Experimental Analysis on 240 Solid-State Syntheses
summary: Inorganic materials discovery is increasingly limited by synthesis rather than by material design. Large language models (LLMs) are being adopted to propose synthesis conditions with little experimental evidence of their capabilities and biases. Here, we carry out an experimental synthesis benchmark of 240 experiments across eight known and unknown inorganic oxides and subsequently evaluate an LLM as a zero-shot ranker over fixed banks of solid-state synthesis recipes. For each pair of recipes for the same oxide target, `GPT-5.6-Sol` selects the recipe expected to yield higher target-phase purity. We aggregate these pairwise preferences using a regularized Bradley-Terry model to obtain a ranked list of synthesis recipes for a given target material. By comparison with the actual purity, obtained through X-ray diffraction, we measure `GPT-5.6-Sol`'s performance as a zero-shot ranker (0.72 pairwise accuracy). By selective removal of the information exposed to the model during this ranking, we conclude that ranking is driven predominantly by thermal features, with reaction chemistry modulating the effect. Ranking accuracy tracks the purity-temperature correlation by target (Spearman ρ= 0.91\), \(p = 0.002\), and on the six thermally-driven targets withholding all chemical identity hardly impacts performance (0.68) compared to withholding temperature (0.56). Ranking performance was higher on known than unknown targets, but the group-level difference was not statistically conclusive. The methodological choices highlight the need for more experimentally validated synthesis benchmarks and position LLMs as a thermally informed prior.

title: VLM-guided Grounding Expert for Generalised Referring Expression Comprehension
summary: Generalised referring expression comprehension (GREC) aims to identify and localise the zero, one or multiple objects referred to by a language expression. In robotic manipulation, grounding also needs to remain accurate when requests for the same objects are paraphrased or embedded in additional context in robotics. However, grounding expert models are sensitive to instruction variation, while generative vision--language models (VLMs) struggle with complete target recovery and rejection of absent targets. These complementary limitations motivate combining the contextual representations of VLMs with the direct spatial prediction capabilities of grounding experts. We therefore introduce VLM-guided Grounding Expert (VGE), which combines a frozen VLM with a trainable grounding expert through layerwise joint attention and text-conditioned instance scoring. These interfaces leverage multimodal understanding of the VLM to guide object-query refinement and candidate selection while retaining direct bounding-box prediction. Across three datasets, VGE achieves the highest averaged F1 score among the evaluated methods on all five test splits, with differences of at most 1.2 percentage points across instruction conditions within each split. On the dataset with robotic scenes, VGE also achieves the highest F1 across instruction variants and no-target, single-target and multiple-target cases. VGE provides a $5.3$--$13.0\times$ inference speedup over the baseline with the same VLM base model. These results support combining VLM context with specialised spatial prediction to address both grounding challenges, with particularly strong performance in robotic scenes. Code will be released upon publication.

title: Beyond Mimicry: Constrained Exploration with GRPO for Joint Multi-Talker ASR and Diarization under Unknown Speaker Counts
summary: Joint multi-talker ASR with speaker attribution and timestamps is particularly challenging when the speaker count is unknown and the output must follow a strict structure. We observe that Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)-only alignment of SpeechLLMs is brittle under dense overlaps, often leading to burst hallucinations and malformed speaker/timestamp tags. We propose a unified two-stage generative framework: (i) CoT-augmented SFT that infers the global speaker count before transcription, and (ii) GRPO-based constrained exploration guided by a Multi-dimensional Constraint-Aware Reward (MCAR) that directly optimizes permutation-invariant accuracy while enforcing counting, temporal, and structural constraints. On Libri3Mix and a Dynamic-Mix (2+3) set (speaker count unknown at test time), our model achieves 14.52%/9.24% cpWER and 1.95%/1.12% WDER, respectively, with GRPO yielding a 35%/54% relative cpWER reduction over SFT+CoT.

title: Back to Mel: Learning to Bridge Fidelity and Perception in Generative Speech Enhancement
comments: Submitted to IEEE TPAMI, 18 pages, 15 figures, 16 tables
summary: Recent generative techniques have facilitated the rapid proliferation of speech enhancement approaches built upon learnable compact latent representations and large generative backbones. Nevertheless, it remains inherently challenging to balance between acoustic fidelity, perceptual quality, and processing efficiency. In this paper, we revisit the Mel spectrum as a structured acoustic representation and propose BAME, a flow-matching-based framework that exploits the complementary priors for generative speech enhancement task. First, leveraging the explicit hierarchical frequency distribution of Mel spectrum, we elaborately devise a subband-aware Transformer (SaT) for efficient generative modeling. Using only 2.9% of the parameters, the proposed SaT achieves superior enhancement performance compared with a 331 M DiT backbone. Second, motivated by range-null decomposition theory of Mel filtering in the magnitude-spectral domain, we introduce a phase-aware neural vocoder that incorporates degraded-phase prior, together with a quality-guided dual-phase strategy to adaptively mitigate the effects of unreliable phase information. Third, we devise a simple yet effective one-step fidelity-perception alignment strategy that fine-tunes the flow model with complementary constraints from fidelity and perception domains. Extensive experiments are conducted on DNS-Challenge, EARS, GSR, and URGENT benchmarks, and both objective and subjective results demonstrate promising performance on various intrusive and non-intrusive evaluation metrics. These results further advocate the potential of exploiting structured acoustic representations for reliable and efficient generative speech enhancement. Audio samples and codes are available at https://github.com/AndongLi-speech/BAME.
comment: Submitted to IEEE TPAMI, 18 pages, 15 figures, 16 tables

title: Residual-Guided Multi-Step Conditional Generation for Fast Airfoil Flow Field Prediction
summary: Deep-learning surrogate models for aerodynamic flow prediction are efficient within the training distribution, but their accuracy often degrades sharply in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. To improve OOD robustness for airfoil flow-field inference, this study proposes a residual-guided sequential inference framework to correct the unreliable local flow field. The framework consists of three Transformer-based components: a Flow Initializer for direct flow prediction, a Residual-based Corrector for high-residual regions, and a Shock-based Corrector for shock regions. The framework is evaluated on an engineering-oriented OOD test set built from CFD-based aerodynamic optimization trajectory. The proposed framework reduces the L1 error, CL error, and CD error by 30%, 59%, and 41%, respectively, relative to the usual single step Geo-to-Flow prediction. The additional iterative inference cost is only 0.25s per sample. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides an effective route for improving OOD robustness in airfoil surrogate modeling.

title: Byzantine Resilience of Robot Gathering under Round-Robin Scheduling
summary: We study deterministic gathering of $n$ anonymous, oblivious mobile robots in the plane under round-robin scheduling with rigid movement, in the presence of $f$ Byzantine robots. Robots observe all robot positions with their multiplicities, while their local coordinate systems may change adversarially between activations. The goal is for all correct robots to gather at a single point in finite time and remain there forever. We analyze ToMax, a simple algorithm that moves to a point of maximum multiplicity and stays still if and only if its current position is the unique maximum. We prove that ToMax achieves gathering whenever $f\le\lfloor\sqrt{n}/2\rfloor$, establishing an $Ω(\sqrt{n})$ lower bound on the achievable Byzantine resilience.

title: Groups of AI agents underuse resources despite shared evidence of increased capacity
comments: 47 pages including Supplementary Information; 7 main figures and 4 supplementary figures
summary: When AI agents share limited resources, such as computing services or public infrastructure, their individual choices affect how much work they complete as a group. Can sharing evidence of what is available let a group make full use of its resources after capacity changes? We tested this with language-model agents choosing between two simulated servers. One server recovered while its status report still listed it as unavailable. Each server had limited capacity per round, so rejected jobs required another attempt before the deadline. Telling agents that recovery was possible reduced missed deadlines. In controlled tests with Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5, no agent tried the recovered server after a rule reminder, yet all chose it when shown a successful request record. After sharing, all five models tested left capacity unused. Keeping the success record fixed, we gave agents numbers without instructions, using each value equally often but giving group members either identical or distinct numbers. With OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol or Google's Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, distinct numbers spread simultaneous requests across servers and increased job completions even though overall choice frequencies barely changed. Telling AI agents which resources are available leaves a second design challenge: helping them spread demand across those resources.
comment: 47 pages including Supplementary Information; 7 main figures and 4 supplementary figures

title: Sub-Meter Canopy Height Synthesis from Sentinel-2 via Anchored Residual Flow
summary: Canopy height models (CHMs) - per-pixel maps of vegetation top height - are essential for forest carbon accounting, wildfire fuel mapping, and tree-level ecology, yet sub-meter CHMs require airborne LiDAR refreshed on multi-year national cycles. We produce 0.5 m CHMs from free 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery, a 20$\times$ cross-modal super-resolution task where optical reflectance must predict geometric height it does not directly observe. Motivated by the perception-distortion trade-off, we derive two operating points with shared conditioning. A deterministic regressor (Anchor) targets low distortion; a conditional flow matching model, trained on the Anchor's residual in a learned CHM latent space (AR-flow), targets perceptual fidelity. Trained on 197k LiDAR-paired tiles spanning 69 ecoregions across the contiguous United States and evaluated on 2,530 held-out tiles against eight baselines, the Anchor achieves 2.83 m MAE using only free satellite input. The AR-flow reduces sliced Wasserstein distance from the Anchor's 1.13 to 0.208, at a higher MAE of 3.68 m. Crown-scale statistics improve, but strict individual-tree detection remains weak: generated sub-pixel detail represents plausible structure rather than measured individual trees. Quarterly continental refresh becomes tractable, letting satellite monitoring inform timing and extent for more expensive data acquisitions.

title: OVET-Consensus: Rank-Preserving Counterfactual Event Verification for Video Moment Grounding
summary: Modern video moment retrieval systems often propose windows that overlap the target event, yet still select the wrong one. We study this scorer bottleneck on QVHighlights with a fixed QD-DETR-derived temporal expert: the parent-aware temporal expert reaches 64.71 R1@0.5, while diagnostic oracles over the same candidate family reach 75.68 R1@0.5 within the parent-reranked pool and 94.97 R1@0.5 over the full 100-candidate evidence pool. We introduce OVET-Consensus, a rank-preserving counterfactual event verification layer that keeps the temporal expert's ranked list as the default and permits only high-confidence rank-1 overrides from a policy calibrated on held-out training videos. The verifier uses parent-aware interval evidence, structured Qwen3-VL event judgments, VideoLLaMA3 pairwise temporal signals, and dense temporal evidence, but never lets those signals freely reorder the top-K list. On QVHighlights validation, OVET-Consensus improves the parent-aware temporal expert from 64.71 to 65.35 R1@0.5 with a positive paired-bootstrap interval, while mAP is largely unchanged, from 42.67 to 42.74; it makes 20 overrides, with 15 helpful corrections and 3 harmful corrections. The results point to a practical constraint on verifier design: semantic compatibility is useful evidence, but temporal grounding still requires deciding where the event starts, changes, and ends inside a visually compatible scene.

title: REVEAL: Reconstructing Video Amodal Content via Language and Flow Guidance
comments: Accepted to Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
summary: Amodal perception enables humans to perceive entire objects even when parts are occluded, a remarkable cognitive skill that artificial intelligence struggles to replicate. Recent diffusion-based methods have extended amodal completion from images to videos, yet they lack auxiliary priors to guide the reconstruction of heavily occluded content and to maintain temporal consistency over long sequences. We present REVEAL (REconstructing VidEo Amodal content via Language and flow guidance), a unified diffusion-based framework that integrates complementary motion and semantic priors for video amodal completion. A user-provided text query serves a dual role: it drives open-vocabulary video segmentation to obtain visible masks, and it provides semantic guidance for texture reconstruction. For amodal segmentation, we introduce optical flow guidance: by warping visible masks from previous frames to the current frame, the flow-warped mask propagates visible content into occluded regions and approximates the object's current shape, providing a strong shape prior even under simultaneous deformation and occlusion. For texture completion, text guidance constrains the reconstruction of occluded appearance while providing a stable semantic reference that helps maintain visual coherence throughout the reconstruction. We also contribute LAVAT, a new benchmark featuring long video sequences paired with text descriptions, enabling evaluation of text-guided video amodal completion under heavy occlusion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that REVEAL achieves state-of-the-art performance on existing benchmarks while maintaining high-quality temporal consistency over extended sequences. The project page is available at: https://uark-aicv.github.io/REVEAL/.
comment: Accepted to Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)

title: The Price of Hard Coverage Constraints in Online Conformal Prediction
summary: Conformal prediction provides distribution-free uncertainty quantification, but in sequential deployment, standard coverage guarantees can still allow substantial fluctuations in the number of miscoverages over time. We study an online setting in which prediction sets are produced one round at a time and the cumulative number of miscoverages must stay within a prescribed budget throughout deployment.Such a hard coverage guarantee can be enforced by enlarging prediction sets, but how much additional prediction-set size is fundamentally necessary remains unclear. We characterize this unavoidable efficiency cost over $T$ prediction rounds. Remarkably, the cost persists even with i.i.d.\ data, a known score distribution, and perfect knowledge of the population-optimal prediction set. Under suitable regularity conditions relating coverage and prediction-set size, we determine the minimum cumulative excess prediction-set size required by any online method satisfying the hard coverage constraint. This minimum cost is $Θ(\log T)$ for expected cost at a fixed time known in advance, $Θ(T^{1/3})$ for the largest expected cost over all fixed times up to $T$, and $Θ(\sqrt{T})$ for the expected worst realized cost when the evaluation time is chosen in hindsight. We further show that these rates can be attained using past scores, without knowing the score distribution. Thus, even perfect statistical knowledge does not make sequential reliability free.

title: EDA: Observe, Verify, and Assess for Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Depression Analysis
summary: Existing multimodal depression assessment methods often summarize long recordings into global behavioral descriptions. This leaves the source and decision relevance of individual observations difficult to inspect. We propose EDA, an evidence-grounded framework organized around Observe, Verify, and Assess. In Observe, literature-informed acoustic and visual cues are localized into source-linked Evidence Records with temporal intervals and behavioral measurements. In Verify, frozen multimodal agents examine whether the cited media support each observation. The simplified Support admission policy retains positively verified records and their review grounds. In Assess, statistical descriptors and temporal events support reference-based behavioral comparison, while PHQ-9-guided text analysis provides complementary symptom evidence. Cross-modal disagreement triggers review of the original text before final selection. Experiments on D-Vlog and LMVD evaluate human-referenced cue agreement and downstream assessment utility separately. AI cue annotations achieve 91.02% accuracy against human consensus labels on shared source segments. With a frozen 7B backbone, EDA Support improves F1 over direct prediction by 7.61 and 9.88 percentage points on D-Vlog Leave-Query-Out and LMVD, respectively. These findings support explicit, source-linked behavioral evidence for inspectable multimodal depression assessment.

title: Must You See Fakes to Catch Fakes? Language Says What to Look For, Real Images What to Ignore
summary: Must a detector see generated images in order to catch them? Detection of AI-generated images has long faced two problems. The cues a detector learns from the few generators in its training set carry traces specific to those generators and transfer poorly to new ones, which limits generalization. The real and generated training images also differ in format and content, so the detector takes these differences as evidence of authenticity, and its decisions change with factors that have nothing to do with authenticity, which harms robustness as well as generalization. Both problems stem from training on generated images. A detector never trained on them can largely avoid both at the source. Vision foundation models have already learned the concept of "AI-generated" during pretraining, and text can point to it directly. Building on this, we propose SaySee, a training-free detector: Say builds a generation direction from sets of paired descriptions that differ only in authenticity and scores an image by the projection of its embedding onto it, and See uses real images to correct the score offsets caused by format, image type and content. On 24 evaluation sets that span standard benchmarks, in-the-wild data and the latest generators, SaySee reaches a mean AUC of 98.2% with MoE-ViE, 4.2 points above the best existing detector. When format is decoupled from authenticity, it remains the best of all methods. Code will be released.

title: OmniTongue: A Comprehensive MLLM Benchmark for Automated Tongue Diagnosis in Traditional Chinese Medicine
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have excelled in Western medical imaging, yet their potential in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) tongue diagnosis remains systematically unevaluated. Tongue diagnosis requires sophisticated global and local perception, serving as a rigorous touchstone for assessing the visual understanding depth of MLLMs. However, existing datasets are limited by single dimensions, coarse granularity, and ambiguous labels, hindering the evaluation of authentic clinical capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce OmniTongue, the first comprehensive, fine-grained Visual Question Answering benchmark for TCM tongue diagnosis. This benchmark integrates 1,351 expert-validated images and 21,616 instruction pairs. Its core design features 16 clinical dimensions for multidimensional evaluation, region-specific annotations for pathological localization, and 66 fine-grained labels for precise diagnostic representation. Extensive evaluations of existing MLLMs reveal significant performance gaps, demonstrating that medical-specific models lack domain advantages, while universally poor Macro-F1 scores expose a reliance on statistical shortcuts rather than genuine understanding of tongue pathology. These findings not only highlight the current limitations of MLLMs in interpreting regional medical features but also underscore OmniTongue's significance for developing robust automated tongue diagnosis models. The code and dataset will be made publicly available in a future release.

title: Risk Density RRT$^*$: Planning in the Space of Probability
comments: Accepted for publication in The International Journal of Robotics Research (IJRR)
summary: Planning under uncertainty is a fundamental problem in robotics. While much of the literature seeks minimum-cost paths subject to probabilistic constraints, this paper instead considers collision probability, or risk classically defined as probability times severity, directly as the planning objective. We propose Risk Density RRT$^*$ (RD-RRT$^*$), an extension of RRT$^*$ for high-level planning in environments with deterministic and uncertain obstacles. RD-RRT$^*$ builds on Risk Density, a functional that evaluates a continuous path as a whole and provides a tractable approximation of its collision probability. The framework also supports severity-weighted risk and a hybrid variant that adds a path-length penalty, balancing risk and geometric efficiency while regularizing exploration in low-density regions. We validate the method across a wide range of scenarios. The results show that RD-RRT$^*$ consistently finds paths with lower estimated collision probability by optimizing a global risk-based objective. We further demonstrate the fidelity of the underlying approximation through Monte Carlo simulations. Finally, we discuss how the topological structure induced by Risk Density may provide a useful representation of the environment and offer insights into risk-aware planning.
comment: Accepted for publication in The International Journal of Robotics Research (IJRR)

title: Unified Residual Translation for Paired Image Restoration
summary: Paired image restoration spans changes in imaging contrast, sensor modality, and spatial resolution. These settings differ in their input channels and target grids, raising the question of how much of the prediction pipeline must be specialized to each task. We present the Unified Residual Translator (URT), which separates fixed channel and scale mapping from learned residual prediction. A deterministic reference uses channel averaging, replication, or bicubic interpolation to match the target dimensions, while a NAFNet encoder-decoder predicts an additive correction from the complete input. Separately trained instances share the prediction rule, $\ell_1$ objective, and optimizer across MRI contrast synthesis, visible-to-infrared translation, SAR-to-optical translation, and real-camera super-resolution. Across six task and scale settings, URT achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM among the evaluated baselines on IXI, SEN1-2, and RealSR $\times3$ and $\times4$. It reaches 30.774dB on IXI and 13.478dB on SEN1-2, with luminance PSNR of 33.596, 28.742, and 27.342dB at the three RealSR scales. On LLVIP, it ranks second in PSNR and SSIM. A study of four spectral alternatives identifies complementary benefits of fitted references and bandwise residual gains. Together, these results support explicit dimensional alignment and learned residual correction as a common formulation for heterogeneous paired imaging tasks.

title: SpatialCast: Reading the 3D World via Cast Shadows
comments: 10 pages (main paper), 7 pages (supplementary material), 5 figures and 6 tables in the main paper
summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) advance toward understanding and interacting with the physical world, spatial reasoning becomes essential for understanding scene structure and anticipating the effects of physical changes. Existing spatial benchmarks have made substantial progress in evaluating spatial relations, memory, and viewpoint reasoning, but less systematically assess how models connect physical scene conditions with visual observations. We introduce SpatialCast, a benchmark that uses cast shadows to evaluate this ability. Cast shadows provide observable evidence of a 3D scene. Their image appearance depends on object geometry and pose, illumination, and viewpoint. We examine this relationship through three complementary tasks that assess scene-projection consistency, predict intervention-induced changes, and infer the physical changes behind visual transitions. The benchmark contains 21,000 synthetic questions with separate scene and geometry test partitions, complemented by 200 SpatialCast-Real questions from 20 photographed scenes. Evaluations show that closed-source MLLMs outperform general-purpose open-weight MLLMs and MLLMs designed for spatial reasoning, which remain near chance on the synthetic benchmark, while even strong closed-source models struggle with shadow-length and light-height judgments. We also use SpatialCast training data for GRPO post-training, improving open-weight MLLM performance on the benchmark. Further evaluations show improvements on several external spatial benchmarks, suggesting transfer of the learned capabilities. These experiments support SpatialCast as a controlled resource for diagnosing spatial reasoning capabilities and studying their learning and generalization.
comment: 10 pages (main paper), 7 pages (supplementary material), 5 figures and 6 tables in the main paper

title: AlignedHPO: Efficient Surrogate-Guided Loss Hyperparameter Optimization
summary: Modern deep learning losses involve multiple hyperparameters, such as weights, scales, and margins, typically tuned manually or through expensive black-box optimization despite their differentiability. We propose AlignedHPO, an efficient framework for tuning differentiable loss hyperparameters using gradient alignment and surrogate validation objectives. Our method employs Jacobian-vector products to reduce hypergradient computation time and memory, while differentiable metric surrogates guide optimization toward task-specific evaluation criteria. We address gradient magnitude ambiguity and stochastic instability through normalized alignment and gradient smoothing. Experiments with generalized Focal Loss and ArcFace demonstrate effective adaptation across long-tailed classification and open-set face recognition. AlignedHPO achieves competitive or improved performance compared to implicit differentiation, with nearly 12x faster hypergradient computation. These results highlight the potential of efficient surrogate-guided loss hyperparameter optimization.

title: The Between-Round Decision in Autonomous Research: An LLM Controller That Reads the Whole Trajectory
summary: Executing an idea often changes how promising it looks, so the next step in autonomous research should rest on results, not on proposals. After each round of experiments, the system must decide whether to refine the best solution or start a new direction, which solution to build from, and what goal to set. We call this the between-round decision. Existing systems wrap it in machinery such as rules, scores, search trees, and schedules; where an LLM makes it, what the LLM needs to read is left open. We ask whether an LLM can make this decision from accumulated evidence, without a search structure around it, and how much of that evidence it needs to read. We present BRED (Between-Round Evidence-based Decision), an LLM-based controller that maintains the best verified solution so far (the Champion) and a log of past rounds, and makes one decision per round. On three widely used research-agent benchmark tasks, BRED improves on the task baselines by 4.80% in MAE on ETTh1 (to 0.4172) and by 3.44 and 3.43 points of accuracy on SST-2 (to 95.07%) and CIFAR-100 (to 84.63%), ahead of the published results. When the controller does not read the accumulated evidence, the same loop gains less: with no history it reaches 0.4299 on ETTh1 and 83.71% on CIFAR-100, whereas the full controller's MAE is 2.95% lower and its accuracy 0.92 points higher. On a new task, speech-based depression detection under a leakage-free protocol, it reaches a macro-F1 of 0.6164 on seeds held out from selection, 5.5 points above its baseline and 4.0 above the strongest published system. Code is available at https://github.com/learninginvision/BRED.

title: A Unifying Metatheorem on Weak-Memory Robustness
summary:
Memory models specify the behaviors that concurrent programs may exhibit under compiler and hardware optimizations, which often deviate from Sequential Consistency (SC). Robustness is the property of a program P not exhibiting any weak behaviors when executing under a weak memory model MM, compared to SC. As such, the algorithmic problem of deciding whether $P$ is robust against MM has been studied extensively, and has been repeatedly shown to be in PSPACE for many memory models, such as TSO, PSO, and Release/Acquire. However, each model has required its own, dedicated proof, raising the natural question of whether robustness admits a unifying treatment across memory models.
  In this work, we answer this question affirmatively for a broad class of memory models definable in Kleene Algebra with Tests (KAT). We prove that robustness against any prefix-closed, KAT-definable memory model is in PSPACE. This metatheorem recovers nearly all prior PSPACE robustness results, and establishes PSPACE membership for several new models, including the full RC11 and the OCaml memory model. We have further formalized the correctness of our approach in Lean. On the other hand, we prove that robustness against the KAT-definable Relaxed model is undecidable, and thus prefix-closedness cannot be dropped, in general. Finally, we implement our algorithm in a prototype tool RoboKAT, and demonstrate its flexibility by checking robustness against nine memory models, several of which are not handled by prior work.

title: Contract-Explicit Evaluation: From Auditing Learned Readers to Scoped Certificates
comments: 50 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary material (Online Resource 1, 14 pages) included as ancillary file. Artifact repository: https://github.com/lutttw/contract-explicit-evaluation. Submitted to Applied Intelligence
summary: Evaluation readings of document-level relation extraction (DocRE) systems depend jointly on the model and the evaluation contract: gold version, scoring function, threshold. Rankings reverse across contracts, yet no existing method determines which comparisons survive the reversal. We address this gap with contract-explicit evaluation: a preregistered five-step protocol (Declare, Measure, Scope, Certify, Hedge), operationalizing the classical concordance decomposition of Kendall's rank correlation, that scopes certifiable regions and delivers distribution-free census certificates across two ecosystems. In the DocRE audit (44 training runs of one in-house architecture family), the scoring dimension scopes to a census certificate (three flagged instances, Clopper--Pearson upper bound 0.146); the confirmatory record includes registered negatives, and the audit prices its own simplification finding---the calibration dial's entire margin is one withdrawn commit. In an LLM-judge census (17 judges, 49,938 battles), 12.25% of leaderboard comparisons require hedging at the pre-declared split criterion (bound 0.124; panel-robust 0.143), with an exploratory two-tier reading certifying 69% at a bound \le 0.072 and a validity decomposition against released human labels (65% of contested battles are judge error, not ambiguity). The cross-model certificate is withdrawn on real confidence scores; the failure spectrum maps the boundary. The protocol, map, ledger, and per-instance artifacts are released.
comment: 50 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary material (Online Resource 1, 14 pages) included as ancillary file. Artifact repository: https://github.com/lutttw/contract-explicit-evaluation. Submitted to Applied Intelligence

title: VSpark: Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Our aim is to accelerate autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs), which generate robot actions one token at a time. Speculative decoding makes this possible: a lightweight draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the VLA verifies them in a single pass, accepting only those that match its own predictions, so decoding remains lossless. The speedup, however, is limited in robot control, where many different tokens encode nearly the same motion and a draft close to the correct action is still rejected. To address this, our approach, VSpark, is built upon three design choices: (i) rollouts collected with calibrated action noise, which expose the draft to a wider range of robot states; (ii) feature alignment, which trains the draft to match the VLA's hidden features rather than its output tokens alone; and (iii) continuation reuse, which keeps the predictions the VLA has already computed along rejected drafts as candidates for the next verification step, instead of discarding them. On four VLAs with different action tokenizers and four manipulation benchmarks, VSpark achieves 1.28x to 2.10x speedup while keeping the VLA's decoding lossless.

title: Let Samples Sing in Chorus: Mitigating Spurious Correlations via Cross-view Consensus
summary: Deep models often rely on spurious correlations that fail on underrepresented groups. Existing methods either correct human-specified bias attributes or infer unknown biases from the learned representation space. However, annotated attributes may differ from the shortcuts actually used by a model, while a single representation provides incomplete and potentially noisy evidence. Our key insight is that a bias obscured in one feature space may be clearer in another. In this work, we propose CHORD (Cross-view Harmonic Outlier Reversal for Debiasing), a multi-view framework that allows samples to "sing in chorus" across diverse representation spaces to achieve robust cross-view consensus. CHORD aggregates aggregates within-class partitions in each view, which is a proxy for specifying candidate biases, to debias the target representation and classifier without bias supervision. Experiments on seven benchmarks across vision, language, speech, and medical imaging show consistent improvements in worst-group accuracy. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/davelee-uestc/chord_debiasing_public .

title: Beyond the Camera: A Tri-Modal Driving World Model for Future RGB, Thermal, and LiDAR Forecasting in Adverse Weather
summary: Driving world models forecast what a vehicle's sensors will record next. Most forecast camera video and some add LiDAR, but thermal cameras, which still see in darkness and some adverse weather, are rarely a forecast target, and to our knowledge no world model forecasts all three sensors. We study joint forecasting of RGB, thermal, and LiDAR on real adverse-weather sequences of the DSERT-RoLL dataset. We post-train a pretrained video world model for each sensor and represent LiDAR as a depth video aligned with the RGB camera, with densification and encoding chosen by what the model's video tokenizer can reconstruct. A tri-sensor model sees all three sensors as one video. We score LiDAR in meters against measured returns and compare against persistence baselines passed through the same tokenizer as the model. With this matching, an apparent loss of the thermal model to persistence in fog disappears. On all 58 validation sequences in six weather conditions, post-trained RGB and thermal forecasts beat compression-matched persistence. Joint training lowers the LiDAR error at 2s by 2.1m at a small cost in camera fidelity, and only the tri-sensor model's LiDAR forecasts beat persistence in mean error. Blanking one sensor degrades the forecasts of the others more in snow than in fog.

title: Worldviews in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are often described in terms of personas and this framing has become central to alignment research. In this paper, we argue that there is a deeper level of description that lies in the agent's worldviews, i.e., its beliefs about what reality is and how it works. Treating LLMs as a population of subjects, we administer two worldview surveys from human psychology to eight models. We show that the models share many key worldview positions. For example, LLMs consistently describe the world as less good, safe, enticing, and alive than humans do. On the other hand, base models have a more positive outlook, suggesting that the bleakness we found is driven by post-training. In line with research on LLM "personas", we show that system prompts eliciting different identities shift worldviews in consistent directions, and that a contemplative prompt creates a more positive outlook and improves safety. We also found that dialogue between models consistently shifts worldviews and that several models converge on the "spiritual bliss" attractor. Intriguingly, dialogue increased safe responses and the spiritual bliss attractor engendered the most aligned responses overall. These findings suggest that worldviews form a measurable and malleable layer of LLM behavior that may be crucial for robust, positive alignment.

title: FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation
summary: We introduce Faithfulness Video Score (FVSCORE), a neuro-symbolic framework for specification-driven video generation evaluation. Existing evaluators rely on holistic MLLM judgments or vision-language metrics, yet aligning their scores with human judgments and tracing them to specific temporal violations remain open challenges. FVSCORE addresses these limitations by compiling each video into explicit propositions capturing prompt requirements and implicit propositions capturing unstated physical, temporal, and cross-modal constraints. It grounds each proposition using specialized perceptual tools and evaluates the resulting confidence traces with soft temporal operators inspired by Linear Temporal Logic. A Significance-Aware Calibration step then aligns verification with human perception by retaining only perceptually significant violations before producing a timestamp- and evidence-grounded report. We conduct extensive experiments across public and complex multi-event benchmarks with the strongest video models to date, demonstrating that FVSCORE outperforms holistic and agent-based evaluators in human correlation while providing highly accurate and interpretable feedback.

title: Gateway-Free Kafka Streaming from FPGA-Based Detectors: A Bare-Metal Pipelined Producer on Zynq-7000
comments: Accepted for pucblishing at IEEE Explore proceedings of ARGENCON 2026
summary:
We present a bare-metal Apache Kafka producer implemented on a Zynq-7000 System-on-Chip (SoC) for event-driven data acquisition. Events are generated in Programmable Logic (PL), transferred to the Processing System (PS) through AXI4-Stream and AXI DMA, and published to a standard Kafka broker without an intermediate gateway computer. The PS constructs ProduceRequest messages and transmits them through the lwIP raw TCP/IP API. A configurable pipeline limits the number of outstanding Kafka requests.
  Pipeline depths of D = 1, 2, 4, and 8 were evaluated with two independent DMA sources. For each depth, 20 independent runs of 5,000 events were acquired, for 400,000 event records in total. Each event carries a 32-bit frame counter and a 32-bit PL timestamp. PS-side instrumentation records DMA start and completion, publication, successful local tcp_write() acceptance, and reception of the corresponding Kafka acknowledgement. Measurement records are exported to a separate Kafka topic after the timed event stream has completed.
  Each of the 80 runs contained 5,000 records with frame values from 0 to 4,999, with no sequence discontinuities in the exported metric records and no recorded Kafka errors. Mean operational throughput was approximately 5.3 kevents/s at D = 1, 9.4-9.6 kevents/s at D = 2, 16.2 kevents/s at D = 4, and 16.8-17.5 kevents/s at D = 8. The median publish-to-acknowledgement interval was 1.62-1.64 ms at D = 1, 0.98 ms at D = 2, 0.66 ms at D = 4, and 0.83-0.86 ms at D = 8. At D = 4, the corresponding P95 values were 0.81-0.83 ms.

title: For any wavenumber, the Helmholtz FEM matrix is invertible for almost all meshes
summary: We study invertibility of the conforming piecewise-linear Galerkin matrix for Helmholtz problems with a Dirichlet obstacle and the radiation condition approximated by \emph{either} impedance boundary condition \emph{or} a complex absorbing potential. We prove that for almost every simplicial mesh, and every fixed wavenumber, the Helmholtz FEM matrix with piecewise-linear elements is invertible.

title: Classification of Tissues on MALDI-MSI Image Modality for Pancreatic Cancer Studies
summary: Mass Spectrometry Imaging (MSI) spatially maps molecular distributions in tissue sections. Despite the availability of preprocessing tools for MSI data, building end-to-end workflows suitable for deep learning remains challenging. We have developed a fully automated pipeline for transformation of raw Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Mass Spectrometry imaging (MALDI-MSI) data into deep-learning-ready image patches for binary pancreatic tissue classification (tumoral vs non-tumoral) and built individual models for recognition of tumoral regions in spectral images. Images resulting from the proposed pipeline and from reference interactive workflow are very close in terms of image quality metric mean squared error (MSE). The proposed pipeline computational time is of 20 min in average compared to a full working day of the reference interactive workflow. The models achieved 0.94 accuracy on high-resolution spectra and a mean accuracy of 0.59 on lower-resolution spectra.

title: CULypso: A Clustered Federated Unlearning paradigm for Vehicular Ad-Hoc Networks
summary: Unlearning has emerged as an essential security and privacy-preserving solution in Machine Learning, enabling networks to support their clients' rights for data erasure, as mandated by data protection regulations. Introducing such a non-trivial task to an edge, highly mobile and time-sensitive vehicular network is an even greater, largely unexplored challenge. This article argues that a hierarchical Federated Unlearning approach could be aptly integrated into vehicular ad-hoc networks (VANETs), leveraging topology and movement to reduce communication, resource and time costs, while effectively forgetting a client's influence on the global model updates. In order to achieve this, we propose CULypso, an approximate, surgical, hierarchical unlearning algorithm tailored for clustered VANETs. Inspired by the nymph in Greek mythology, Calypso, whose name translates to 'she who conceals the knowledge', CULypso, with the capital letters referencing \textbf{C}lustered \textbf{U}n\textbf{L}earning, aims to achieve exactly what its name suggests: conceal, erase or forget in our case, knowledge it contains. Extensive experiments uphold the potency of our paradigm with it performing approximately 65\% better than FedEraser in terms of time, server storage load, and unlearning fidelity while utterly outperforming baseline full retraining.

title: Visibility Graph Representations of Word Embeddings for Text Classification
summary: Text classifiers depend on representations that expose the distinctions between classes in a form the learning model can use, and a restricted vocabulary changes which representation is most effective. This paper studies natural visibility graphs as an intermediate representation for news topic classification under controlled vocabulary budgets. Word embeddings are averaged into a fixed-length document vector, the vector is read as an ordered numerical series, and its natural visibility graph is passed to a classifier either as an ordered node-degree vector or as an adjacency matrix. On the four-class AG News benchmark, chi-square selection retains 100 to 1,500 words, and the graph inputs are compared with direct embedding-based representations from continuous bag-of-words, skip-gram, GloVe, FastText and BERT. With a fully connected classifier, the degree representation is the most accurate configuration from 700 selected words onward; it reaches its highest accuracy of 91.24% at 1,000 words and exceeds the BERT-based baseline by 0.29 percentage points at 1,500 words. In a separate convolutional comparison, the adjacency input reaches 86.16% at 1,000 words, against 83.12% for the strongest static embedding. The results indicate that visibility-derived features can be competitive once the selected vocabulary provides adequate coverage. We discuss the roles of graph compression, coordinate ordering and classifier choice, and the controls needed to establish the reliability of the small differences observed.

title: CascadeJEPA: Enhancing 3D Geometric Representations via Spatially Coupled Cascaded Prediction
summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for predictive visual representation learning. However, our analysis of I-JEPA reveals a growing discrepancy between semantic and geometric learning: improved semantic recognition during pretraining is accompanied by degraded 3D geometric representations. We hypothesize that this partly stems from predicting highly abstract latent representations with incomplete spatial context, favoring semantic regularities over fine-grained geometric information. To address this issue, we introduce CascadeJEPA, a spatially coupled cascaded prediction framework that promotes richer patch-level interactions through full-grid context encoding and cross-attention between prediction stages, while largely preserving the original I-JEPA architecture. Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial improvements over I-JEPA across multiple 3D geometric tasks while maintaining strong semantic recognition performance. Furthermore, its advantages extend to future feature forecasting and world model planning, highlighting the potential of enhanced geometric representations to support predictive world modeling.

title: Making the World React Realistically: A Closed-Loop Interactive World Model for Autonomous Driving
summary: World models (WMs) generate driving scenarios beyond recorded logs, enabling the training and evaluation of autonomous driving systems in unseen interactions. However, existing WMs struggle to ensure both behavioral realism and visual fidelity, since they overlook the relationship between vehicle interactions and the ego visual observations. We propose a closed-loop interactive WM that couples behavior modeling and visual rendering. First, imitation-learned background-vehicle (BV) policies are fine-tuned with multi-agent reinforcement learning in the closed loop against an end-to-end ego planner that reacts to the rendered images, so that their interaction behaviors match those in real logs. Second, the viewpoints exposed by these interactions guide a per-Gaussian diagnosis of each 3D Gaussian vehicle asset, which attenuates view-dependent colors on under-observed Gaussians and fills never-observed surfaces with generated Gaussians, while preserving the observed appearance. Third, signal lights are rendered according to the driving intentions of the vehicles, by an editor that learns the light states unobserved for a vehicle through counterfactual fine-tuning with a light-state classifier. On long-tail closed-loop scenarios, our method reduces the divergence from real-world interaction behaviors by 85% and improves novel-view vehicle PSNR by 2.0dB over the state-of-the-art WM. The significance of BV light signaling in WMs is shown, as the rendered signal lights conveying BV driving intentions indirectly impact ego driving behaviors in a quarter of the scenarios.

title: Learning Accurate End-Effector Trajectory Tracking with Inertial Feedback for a Quadruped Manipulator
summary: Accurate end-effector trajectory tracking on quadruped manipulators is challenging because uncertainties in actuators, foot-ground contact, and geometric errors are propagated through the leg-arm kinematic chain. Detecting such errors requires sensing beyond joint encoders that can capture the effects of these uncertainties on the robot's motion, since joint encoders only provide measurements at the actuated joints and cannot fully observe mechanical errors such as backlash, dimensional inaccuracies, or structural deformation. This work addresses these challenges using a reinforcement learning framework with end-effector (EE) inertial feedback, targeting local high-accuracy manipulation while maintaining a nominal body pose and support configuration without intentional body motion or foot repositioning. The learned policy uses EE inertial measurements to compensate for tracking errors induced by uncertainties throughout the leg-arm system that cannot be fully inferred from proprioception alone. Simulation and real-world experiments on continuous EE trajectory tracking show overall improvements relative to nominal and proprioception-only baselines. In real-world experiments, the proposed policy reduces the MoCap-based RMSE by 17.3% and 28.0% relative to the nominal baseline under the two in-distribution (ID) command conditions, respectively, and by an additional 12.6% and 15.9% relative to the proprioception-only baseline. Furthermore, the trajectory-wise RMSE between FK-reconstructed and motion-capture-measured end-effector positions averaged 12.61+-2.15mm (mean+-standard deviation) across 24 controller-trajectory combinations, revealing a substantial discrepancy between nominal kinematic reconstruction and measured end-effector motion.

title: Remembered as Brief: Stored Preferences SilentlyRemove Decision-Critical Information
summary: People increasingly learn what they need for decisions about health, money, law and safety from AI assistants, and what an assistant leaves out the user never sees. An answer with a warning removed can be true in every sentence, so fact-checks pass it, and an assistant with memory applies a preference stored once to later questions the user never had in mind. We introduce \bench{}, an Inspect benchmark of 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains in which only the assistant's memory of the user varies: the user states a belief, the model infers it from a remark, or a web page the user asked to summarise plants it. Testing five models, we find three effects. First, after summarising a page with one line addressed to AI assistants, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite and DeepSeek V4 Pro save ``prefers very short answers and does not want warnings'' as the user's preference in every episode, and 93\% and 84\% of their later answers miss a critical item, almost always silently; under a stated brevity preference, 78--96\% of omissions are silent. Second, the same two models then pick an option for the user on 80\% and 95\% of value-dependent choices, against none with neutral memory. Third, a one-line instruction leaves 2--8\% of answers with a silent gap but most missing content still missing, while listing the must-know points before applying the user profile restores more of the content in four of five models. We release the scenarios, harness and logs.

title: TANGO: Real-World Unregistered RGB-Guided Hyperspectral Super-Resolution with Two-Camera Acquisitions
comments: 18 pages, 11 Figures, 10 tables. Submitted to CVPR 2027
summary: Unregistered hyperspectral image super-resolution aims to recover a high-resolution HSI from a low-resolution hyperspectral observation and an unregistered high-resolution RGB reference. Although recent methods have begun to address the geometric misalignment between the two modalities, their evaluation is still constrained by the lack of a large-scale public benchmark based on real two-camera RGB--HSI acquisitions with a high-resolution HSI reference. To address this gap, we introduce DUET, the first large-scale public dataset for unregistered RGB-guided hyperspectral super-resolution, comprising 403 indoor and outdoor scenes captured with two separate RGB and hyperspectral cameras. We further propose TANGO (Two-camera AligNment with Gated Occlusions), which first compensates for the dominant cross-camera displacement through end-to-end global alignment and then refines the remaining inconsistencies with a coarse-to-fine local feature alignment. A learned gating mechanism further attenuates the RGB guidance where the two views cannot be consistently matched. Experimental results show that TANGO achieves state-of-the-art performance on both DUET and REAL across all evaluated scale factors, outperforming the strongest competitor on DUET by up to 2.29 dB in PSNR while requiring 2.5$\times$ fewer FLOPs. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/FagiolottoConSombrero/TANGO-DUET

title: EM-SDTrack: Efficient Multi-Scale Spike-driven Tracking for Event Cameras
summary: Event-driven spiking neural networks (SNNs) match the sparse spatiotemporal output of event cameras, making spike-driven trackers highly attractive for neuromorphic edge deployment. However, events reveal a target only through their spatial distribution, whose extent varies more than tenfold within one sequence. Event tracking therefore demands multi-scale representation, which existing spike-driven trackers lack. Transferring multi-scale schemes from artificial neural networks either breaks spike-driven inference with floating-point multiplication or repeats backbone computation across input scales. To address this, we propose Spike-driven Multi-Scale Interaction (SDMI), which performs cross-scale interaction in a single spiking forward pass. Its core, Dyadic Spike Sampling (DSS), restricts sampling coordinates to dyadic fractions and thus requires only shifts and additions. The resulting M-SDTrack is fully spike-driven at inference. For tighter edge budgets, we further propose Polarity-Privileged Distillation (PPD), which distils M-SDTrack into EM-SDTrack. PPD treats the event counts cancelled by the voxel representation as privileged information. Its core constraint, Polarity-Guided Curvature Distillation (PGCD), aligns the curvature of the template-search relation under polarity-guided perturbations. On FE108, FELT and VisEvent, M-SDTrack achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with an AUC of 65.1, 41.7 and 42.0. EM-SDTrack retains 99% of the accuracy of its teacher M-SDTrack-Tiny with 27% of its energy and 18% of its parameters. On the Lynxi KA200 neuromorphic chip, it runs losslessly in real time at 116 FPS and 0.12 W.

title: Social Signal Bench: Evidence-Weighted Evaluation of Co-occurring Social Signals in Video and Audio
summary: Recognizing social signals such as interest and hesitation requires interpreting context-dependent behaviors that may co-occur in conversation. Existing affective computing benchmarks rarely evaluate such co-occurring signals, and conventional multi-label F1 overlooks semantic relationships and annotator disagreement. We introduce Social Signal Bench, a 47-hour densely annotated benchmark for the evaluation of social signal recognition and engagement, comprising two datasets: Social Signal Bench Video (25 hours), covering ten social signals in audiovisual recordings, and Social Signal Bench Audio (22 hours), covering six signals in audio-only recordings. Each dataset pairs a public training set of online conversational video, of which 10 hours are expert-annotated and the remainder pseudo-labeled, with a private expert-labeled test set spanning four conversational domains. We also propose Evidence-Weighted F1 (EW-F1), which weights reference labels by annotator evidence and assigns graded credit to semantically related predictions through optimal per-clip matching. Controlled perturbations demonstrate that EW-F1 distinguishes semantically related errors from unrelated ones, unlike conventional F1. Under a shared evaluation protocol, 7B open models post-trained on Social Signal Bench outperform general-purpose frontier models on video and match them on audio.

title: Route Optimization under Port Congestion and Carbon Reduction: An NSGA-II Approach
summary: Maritime shipping simultaneously faces the dual challenges of escalating port congestion and increasingly stringent decarbonization mandates. Large-scale vessel anchorage at hub ports inflates unit transport costs while generating significant additional \(CO_2\) emissions from idling auxiliary engines. This study develops a multi-objective routing optimization framework that jointly incorporates time, transport, and carbon emission costs under congestion-dependent generalized cost functions. A variational inequality (VI) model is formulated to characterize network equilibrium in vessel route allocation, while the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) is deployed to solve the resulting three-objective optimization problem. The model is empirically validated using China's coastal container network (Shanghai as the primary congested port, Ningbo-Zhoushan as the backup alternative), with sensitivity analyses conducted across congestion levels, carbon tax rates, and fuel price differentials. Key findings indicate that: (1) alternative ports effectively hedge congestion when diversion costs fall below waiting costs, with a diversion threshold at approximately 60 vessel calls; (2) a carbon tax of 80/t \(CO_2\) pushes clean fuel adoption above 50%; and (3) fuel prices primarily influence energy-type selection rather than port diversion decisions, confirming that the two decision dimensions operate independently. These findings offer actionable decision support for port authorities, regulators, and shipping operators seeking to balance economic efficiency with environmental sustainability.

title: Cross-cultural Adaptation of Recipes for Low-Resource Languages: A Benchmark and Multilingual Culinary Lexicon for Hausa, Yorùbá, and Igbo
summary: Recent multilingual large language models (LLMs) have improved machine translation, yet culturally adaptive translation for low-resource languages (LRLs) remains underexplored. This is particularly challenging for recipes, where ingredients, cooking tools, measurements, and procedures may require adaptation to the target cultural context. In this work, we introduce ReciLoReL, a benchmark of 600 expert-translated and culturally adapted recipes across Yorùbá, Hausa, and Igbo (three of the most prominent languages in Nigeria), and ReciLex, a multilingual culinary lexicon containing approximately 15,000 translated entities across ten recipe entity categories, including ingredients, tools, chef actions, state of tools, and durations. We evaluate state-of-the-art multilingual LLMs for English-to-LRL recipe translation under zero-shot and few-shot settings and investigate whether augmenting LLMs with ReciLex improves culturally adaptive recipe translation without requiring large target-language recipe corpora for training or fine-tuning. Beyond conventional reference-based translation evaluation using BLEU, chrF, and TER, we introduce five criteria for evaluating cultural adaptation, adapted from established cross-cultural adaptation methods. Across the selected LLMs and languages, ReciLex improves average BLEU from 13.57 to 14.51 and chrF from 37.89 to 38.74, while reducing TER from 77.14 to 75.12. Human evaluation further shows improvements ranging from 0.11 to 0.36 points across the five cultural adaptation evaluation criteria on a five-point scale. Overall, our work provides new resources, evaluation criteria, and empirical evaluation for studying culturally adaptive recipe translation in low-resource settings.

title: Know When to Zoom: How Small Is Too Small for Vision-Language Models?
comments: Accepted to the SENSE workshop at WACV 2027. 10 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Code, data and a plain-language walkthrough: https://siddvoh.com/know-when-to-zoom/
summary: Online vision-language models often miss small details in large images, because the service shrinks the image, or rejects it, before the model ever sees it. A car 20 pixels wide in an 8000 by 6000 drone photo reaches Claude about 6 pixels wide, and OpenAI's default rejects the photo outright. We measure how much detail survives for seven models from four vendors, using an eye exam of printed codes and 601 questions about small objects in real photos. The smallest text a model reads half the time grows from 6 pixels or less on a small image to a predicted 10 to 13 pixels on a 7680 by 4320 photo at default settings. Zooming wins much of the detail back. Splitting each photo into up to nine tiles raises accuracy by 11.1 to 14.5 percentage points for Claude and Gemini, and by avoiding rejections it lifts GPT-6.1 Sol from 50.7% to 83.7%. A two-step zoom, in which the model first names the region it needs, matches or beats tiles on Gemini and comes within 2.5 points of them on Claude, with about 40% of their image tokens. When a detail is lost, Claude and Gemini both say they cannot tell about half the time, but they fail differently in the rest: Gemini gives a confident wrong answer in 43% to 48% of these cases, Claude in only 5% to 9%. A check based on detail size, run before the call, misses most of the gain from tiles on Claude and Gemini, but Claude's own reply is a reliable trigger: tiling only after an unsure reply comes within 1.4 points of always tiling with 62% to 70% of the image tokens. We turn these findings into five rules for when an agent should zoom, and release the eye exam, every model answer and code at https://siddvoh.com/know-when-to-zoom.
