Prepared with AI assistance (Anthropic Claude for drafting, revision and the verification scripts; OpenAI ChatGPT for a critical reading of a draft); all measurements were produced and verified by the author, who is responsible for the content

title: First Order Geometry of Equilateral Small Polygons
summary:
We develop a first order calculus based on the geometry of realised diameter graphs for perimeter maximisation among convex equilateral small polygons. Polygon side equalities and active diameter constraints define a linearised feasible cone and an associated equality space. We prove that an equilateral small polygon is a strict local maximiser of perimeter modulo Euclidean motions if a multiplier balance holds with strictly positive active diameter multipliers and the active equality space consists only of infinitesimal Euclidean motions. The proof uses a local Euclidean slice and a geometric limiting argument and requires neither independence of the active constraint gradients nor second order information.
  As an application, we combine our criterion with validated interval arithmetic to establish strict local maximality for Bingane and Audet's polygons $A_{16}$, $A_{32}$, $A_{64}$ and for reconstructions of their polygons $Z_{32}$ and $Z_{64}$. For each $n\in\{32,64\}$, the perimeter of $Z_n$ is strictly larger than that of $A_n$. Thus, strict local maximisers with different perimeters coexist in the space of convex equilateral small polygons with the same number of sides.

title: Amortizing Tempered Sampling with Corrected Self-Training
summary: Learning a neural sampler can reduce the cost of repeated sampling from an un-normalized distribution, but obtaining good training data remains difficult. We develop a corrected self-training scheme across a sequence of tempered targets, making use of importance sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo to correct the samples and replay buffers to store them. We introduce Sequential Score Sampler (SSS) as a particular case. In SSS, the proposal is a score-based diffusion trained by regression on energy gradients; and the samples are corrected by importance weights on the path space. After training, samples can be collected directly from the model, from its importance-corrected proposals, or from the final-temperature buffer. The method amortizes repeated sampling by encoding the global structure of the target in the model. SSS achieves competitive sampling accuracy across the benchmarks and, on several targets, uses shorter runtimes with fewer energy evaluations than competing samplers.

title: Insight into Parametric First-Order Ambisonics Upscaling in Time and Frequency Domains
summary: First-Order Ambisonics (FOA) offers a practical representation for spatial audio, but its low-order reproduction introduces distinct perceptual limitations during binaural rendering. While recent methods synthesize Higher-Order Ambisonics (HOA) from FOA to overcome these constraints, the importance and potential of early reflections in the upscaling process have not yet been comprehensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap and understand the potential of incorporating early reflections in FOA upscaling, this work develops an experimental framework that selectively upscales these reflections. By utilizing an energy-based criterion, the proposed framework identifies and selectively renders the strongest early reflections with high-order resolution. The selection mechanism is evaluated across three domains: long-term temporal, short-time temporal, and the joint time-frequency (TF) domain. Validation through objective metrics, including the Scale-Invariant Signal-to-Distortion Ratio (SI-SDR), the clarity index ($C_{50}$), and Interaural Cross-Correlation (IACC), alongside listening tests, demonstrates that the TF-domain provides superior performance. By exploiting the sparsity of speech, the TF approach maintains robust performance in complex multi-talker scenarios, providing insights into the benefits of early reflections for the design of future parametric and data-driven FOA upscaling methods.

title: StreamingDPD: A 1.28-GSa/s Instantaneous-Power-Gated Depthwise TCN Accelerator for Real-Time 320-MHz Digital Predistortion
summary: State feedback between successive samples limits the streaming throughput of recurrent neural networks for digital predistortion (DPD). We present StreamingDPD, an accelerator that processes 320-MHz signals at 1.28 GSa/s. Its 207-parameter instantaneous-power-gated depthwise temporal convolutional network (IPG-DWTCN) uses $|x[n]|^2$ to gate feature channels and causal dilated depthwise convolutions to model power amplifier memory. The network maps to a spatially unrolled fixed-point pipeline with shift-based quadratic activations and layer-wise mixed precision, sustaining one complex sample per cycle per lane. Its algorithmic cost is 554 floating-point operations per complex sample, 30.1% fewer than the recurrent baseline with the best linearization performance. In RF playback measurements on three power amplifiers driven by 40- to 320-MHz Wi-Fi 6/7 and 5G NR waveforms, IPG-DWTCN achieves the lowest mean adjacent-channel power ratio (ACPR) and ranks first or ties for first in mean error vector magnitude (EVM) against five neural baselines of comparable size. Four-lane FPGA hardware-in-the-loop tests on a 320-MHz 4096-QAM Wi-Fi 7 waveform achieve -45.82 dBc ACPR and -42.94 dB EVM at 1.28 GSa/s. At the same sample rate, post-layout evaluation of a single-lane 12-nm FinFET ASIC yields a 0.10 mm$^2$ core, a 52-cycle (40.63 ns) latency, and an estimated typical-corner power of 142.21 mW (111.10 pJ/sample). Relative to the prior 22-nm recurrent DPD ASIC, the design provides 5.1 times the throughput at about one-seventh the energy per sample.

title: Which Past Matters? Training History and Multi-Forecast Horizon in Equity Transformers
summary: More historical data can improve estimation while introducing relationships that transfer poorly to current market conditions. We therefore examine how training quantity and historical selection interact with forecast horizon in intraday equity prediction. We deploy twelve configurations which combine four sampling and validation policies with 6, 12 and 24 month training quantities under a fixed cross-sectional Transformer and feature set. A monthly walk-forward experiment produces 264 refits and eight cumulative return forecasts from 5 to 120 minutes. Evaluation covers January 2025 through 20 October 2026 and uses cross-sectional Spearman information coefficients against future five-factor residual returns. Six-month recency sampling leads individual models at 5-15 minutes, while multi recency configurations lead at 20-30 minutes and uniform configurations at 60-120 minutes. Increasing training quantity does not uniformly improve accuracy while an equal-weight ensemble of all twelve models exceeds every individual mean at 15, 20 and 25 minutes, but not at the remaining horizons. These findings support evaluating historical selection jointly with forecast horizon without identifying a universal policy or a causal benefit from recency.

title: Inference after coding agents
summary: Empirical research is changing rapidly as AI coding agents are becoming increasingly proficient in every step of it, from writing code to manipulating data. We argue that while the potential of coding agents for science is vast, their use in hypothesis testing poses a substantial threat to classical inference, as these agents enable a supercharged form of selective inference. In particular, we argue that coding agents carrying out empirical research introduce a new type of post-selection inference that combines human-like, open-ended search over an implicit space of estimators with programmatic replayability of both the selection and the estimation process. Indeed, we find that on simulated data with zero effects, four frontier agents report significant p-values between 54% and 98% of the time when asked to produce a compelling finding. We propose a simple procedure for detecting and correcting these distortions. After an agent has completed its analysis, we reset and replay it on subsamples of the data to estimate the agent's relative probability of selecting that analysis when it looks statistically favorable. For agents with stable selection behavior, the resulting corrected test is asymptotically valid and consistent conditional on selection. Importantly, the correction is learned from the black-box agent's actual choices rather than a model of how it searches, so it remains valid even as AI technology continues to evolve rapidly. In simulations, the correction robustly lowers the high false rejection rates to near the nominal 5%. We illustrate the method on applications from two published papers.

title: Fully Spiking Neural Implementation of Lambda-Calculus Beta-Reduction via Biologically Documented Mechanisms
summary: We present the first complete implementation of $β$-reduction in the untyped $λ$-calculus using exclusively spiking neural dynamics. Every step of the reduction---redex detection, subterm segmentation, variable-binding detection, De~Bruijn index arithmetic, token copying, and inter-step role maintenance---is performed by leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with explicit membrane dynamics, exponential synaptic currents, axonal delays, and pair-based spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). Each neural component maps onto a specific, experimentally documented mechanism: Jeffress-type delay-line coincidence for redex detection; a line-attractor balance counter for subterm segmentation; $θ$--$γ$ cross-frequency coupling for De~Bruijn variable binding; a phase-ring traveling wave for depth-index arithmetic; theta-cycle STDP for token copying; and recurrent persistent firing for role maintenance between reduction steps. All synaptic weights are derived analytically from measured EPSP amplitudes; no hand tuning is performed. The closed-loop system achieves 100\,\% agreement with a symbolic oracle across ten validation classes, including Church numeral arithmetic (\textsc{plus}, \textsc{mult}, \textsc{pred}), Boolean logic with divergent branches, Y-combinator steps, terms with up to six bound-variable occurrences, De~Bruijn indices up to~12, noise robustness, and determinism. To our knowledge this is the first Turing-complete symbolic computation performed entirely within spike dynamics using biologically grounded circuit primitives. We discuss implications for neuromorphic proof assistants and the neural basis of symbolic reasoning.

title: Integral Tensor Isomorphism via Cubic Rings and Lattice Methods
summary: We prove that isomorphism of integral $2\times3\times3$ tensors under $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ is decidable in bounded-error quantum polynomial time. For a tensor $T=(A,B)$ with nonzero determinant form $\det(xA-yB)$, we use the parametrization of Wood by balanced modules to reduce the isomorphism problem to principality tests for compatible lattices, and use the algorithms of Bley, Hofmann, and Johnston to solve this in BQP. When the determinant form vanishes identically, we get either an integral $2\times2\times2$ core, or a polynomial kernel vector of degree one or two. The linear-kernel case yields another compatible lattice problem, while the quadratic-kernel case reduces to a fixed system of polynomial congruences and unimodular lifting. A quantifier-elimination argument decides these congruences in deterministic polynomial time given the prime factorization of the modulus, which quantum integer factorization supplies. Finally, we show that zero padding preserves integral $2\times2\times2$ tensor isomorphism, yielding a polynomial-time reduction from real-quadratic principality to the identically singular $2\times3\times3$ problem.

title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime
summary: Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved. We couple polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport and surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate. Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation. For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated to take 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Estimated three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits. IBM hardware experiments demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for this wake, using reference circuits to mitigate noise.

title: An inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method for constrained convex finite-sum optimization
comments: Accepted by SIAM Journal on Optimization
summary: In this paper, we study a class of constrained convex finite-sum optimization problems. In many practical applications, all or some of the constraints are hard constraints that represent imperative requirements. Consequently, any desirable approximate solution must (nearly) satisfy these constraints. Motivated by this, we focus on computing an $ε$-$surely\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ ($ε$-SFSO) solution, in which the constraint violation is deterministically bounded by $ε$, and the expected optimality gap is at most $ε$. While a recently proposed stochastic variance-reduced first-order penalty method can compute an $ε$-SFSO solution, there remains a significant gap between its first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution and that for computing an $ε$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, where both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are bounded by $ε$. To narrow this gap, we propose an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) method that significantly improves the previously best-known first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution. Furthermore, when the objective consists of a single function, the proposed method reduces to a novel deterministic first-order method for solving standard convex conic optimization. It achieves a significantly lower gradient evaluation complexity with respect to the objective function compared to existing methods, and can outperform them when computing constraint gradients and projections onto the associated cone is cheaper than evaluating the objective gradient. Preliminary numerical results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed method.

title: StringQFT: A Multiuse Textbook Resource for AI-Assisted Theoretical Physics
comments: 23 pages, 6 figures. Companion paper to an 18-volume textbook collection. Textbook PDFs: https://xingyangyu.com/textbook/
summary: We present StringQFT as a textbook collection for string constructions of quantum field theory and as infrastructure for AI-assisted theoretical physics. The collection comprises 18 volumes, 190 chapters and 3,795 pages, covering brane probes, brane webs, geometric engineering, F-theory constructions, wrapped M5-branes and exact worldsheet constructions. Its open-book benchmark inventory contains 1,073 items, including 499 with automatic finite-answer checking. For retrieval-augmented generation, it provides 1,371 section records linked to textbook sources and PDF locations, together with a local lexical retriever. Training-data preparation is illustrated by 21 private, source-linked examples. For agents, it exposes 19 calculation tools with specified inputs and finite domains, connecting tool use to textbook derivations. We illustrate these uses through specific questions, retrieved passages and finite calculations. The textbook collection and accompanying resources are available at https://github.com/xingyang-yu/StringQFT.

title: Algorithmic Insurance
summary: When artificial intelligence (AI) systems make errors in high-stakes domains such as medical diagnosis or autonomous driving, a single algorithmic flaw across varying contexts can generate heterogeneous losses that challenge traditional insurance assumptions. Algorithmic insurance, financial coverage for AI-induced damages, is an emerging market, yet insurers struggle to price these risks and AI developers lack frameworks linking system design to liability exposure. We connect a key operational choice in binary classification, how practitioners set decision thresholds, to tail risk exposure. Using conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) to capture extreme losses, we prove that established approaches such as accuracy maximization can significantly increase worst-case losses relative to tail risk optimization, with penalties growing at least quadratically as thresholds deviate from optimal. We propose a liability insurance contract that mandates risk-aware thresholds and characterize when it creates value for AI providers, extending the analysis to degrading model performance and human oversight. In a mammography case study, accuracy-maximizing thresholds carry up to four times the tail risk of CVaR-optimal thresholds. Insurance contracts create 7-8% gains for well-calibrated firms through risk transfer and regulatory capital relief, and up to 105% for poorly calibrated firms through mandatory recalibration, while partially aligned firms can lose under a strict mandate, calling for threshold flexibility in contract design. Unlike traditional insurance that merely transfers risk, algorithmic insurance can act as both a financial instrument and an operational governance mechanism, enabling risk transfer while improving AI safety.

title: Smooth Surfaces via Nets of Geodesics
comments: Error in Neumann BC corrected, Numerical experiments revised
summary:
We study the reconstruction of smooth surfaces from networks of spatial curves prescribed as geodesics. Motivated by applications in computer-aided geometric design and the perception of three-dimensional shape, we propose a variational approach minimizing the integral of squared Gaussian curvature over surfaces spanning geodesic contours.
  Using isothermal coordinates, we derive the Euler-Lagrange equation for the conformal factor of the metric and the associated Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions. We also consider a biharmonic approximation obtained by linearizing the nonlinear equation.
  Numerical experiments are performed on four quadrilateral cells of a geodesic network constructed on an ellipsoid. We compute approximate isothermal coordinates, solve the biharmonic boundary-value problem, and compare the resulting curvature with that of the reference surface. These experiments consist of an important step towards a complete framework for the computation of smooth surfaces from geodesic curves.

title: Adaptive mesh refinement for the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation
summary: We propose a new adaptive algorithm for the approximation of the Landau--Lifshitz--Gilbert equation via a higher-order tangent plane scheme. We show that the adaptive approximation satisfies an energy inequality and demonstrate numerically that the adaptive algorithm outperforms uniform approaches.

title: Optimizer's Information Criterion: Dissecting and Correcting Bias in Data-Driven Optimization
summary: In data-driven optimization, the sample performance of the obtained decision typically incurs an optimistic bias against the true performance, a phenomenon commonly known as the Optimizer's Curse and intimately related to overfitting in machine learning. We develop a general approach that we call \emph{Optimizer's Information Criterion (OIC)} to correct this bias. OIC generalizes the celebrated Akaike Information Criterion from the evaluation of model adequacy, used primarily for model selection, to objective performance in data-driven optimization, which is used for decision selection. Our approach analytically approximates and cancels out the bias that comprises the interplay between model fitting and downstream optimization. As such, it saves the computational need to repeatedly solve optimization problems in cross-validation, while operating more generally than other bias approximating scheme. We apply OIC to a range of data-driven optimization formulations comprising empirical and parametric models, their regularized counterparts, and furthermore contextual optimization. Finally, we provide numerical validation of the superior performance of our approach under synthetic and real-world datasets.

title: Joint Communication and Control: Causal Coordination Coding for Witsenhausen Counterexample
comments: Published in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory. Date of publication: 12 October 2026
summary: In decentralized network control, communication plays a crucial role by transforming local observations into shared knowledge, enabling agents to coordinate their actions. This paper investigates how communication facilitates cooperation behavior and therefore improves the overall performance in Witsenhausen counterexample, a canonical toy problem in distributed decision-making. We consider the vector-valued setups where the encoder, i.e., the first decision-maker (DM) acts causally and the decoder, i.e., the second DM, operates noncausally, 1) without and 2) with access to channel feedback. Using a coordination coding framework, we characterize the achievable power-estimation cost regions in single-letter expressions for both scenarios. We show that feedback enlarges the coordination region compared with the no-feedback setup. Building on the characterization of the power-estimation cost region, we propose a hybrid strategy that combines discrete quantization with a continuous Gaussian codebook, the Zero Estimation Cost (ZEC) strategy. This strategy uses coding tools that allow perfect reconstruction of the target symbols, leading to an asymptotic estimation cost equal to zero, while substantially reducing the power cost. Moreover, when channel feedback is available, we propose an analogous ZEC strategy that simultaneously achieves zero power and zero estimation costs in the low-noise regime. Finally, we establish that, when restricted to jointly Gaussian random variables, the performance is identical across all setups featuring at least one causal DM, regardless of the presence of feedback information.

title: A one-dimensional model of catheter aspiration in blood vessels
summary: Aspiration thrombectomy is a primary endovascular treatment option for acute ischemic stroke caused by large vessel occlusions, in which a catheter is navigated to the occlusion site and suction is applied to remove the thrombus. This work introduces a reduced one-dimensional model for aspiration in blood vessels that accounts for the elasticity of both the vessel wall and the catheter. The inclusion of vessel wall visco-elasticity transforms the governing equation for the flow rate into a parabolic form, enabling an accurate resolution of the diffuse pressure gradients near the catheter tip observed in CFD simulations. The numerical treatment is based on a relaxation of the hyperbolic subsystem that facilitates nodal solvers, enabling efficient coupling between catheterized and uncatheterized vessel segments, including bifurcations and the catheter tip. A splitting strategy ensures that the visco-elastic terms incur only negligible additional computational cost relative to the purely hyperbolic model. The model is benchmarked against three-dimensional CFD simulations and reference data from the literature. Numerical experiments investigating the role of catheter elasticity and suction force on the hemodynamics are presented, and an uncertainty quantification study demonstrates the suitability of the framework for efficient parameter studies. The results indicate that the proposed model resolves blood flow comparably accurate to three-dimensional simulations at a fraction of the computational cost. While further in vitro and in vivo validation is required, the framework represents a promising step toward computationally efficient preoperative planning and uncertainty-aware decision support in aspiration thrombectomy.

title: Clustering in pure-attention hardmax transformers and its role in sentiment analysis
comments: Funded by the European Union's HORIZON-MSCA-2021-DN-01-01, through the ModConFlex project ("Modelling and control of flexible structures interacting with fluids''; Grant Agreement No. 101073558; DOI: https://doi.org/10.3030/101073558). Accompanying code available at: https://github.com/DCN-FAU-AvH/clustering-hardmax-transformers, code DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21107513
summary: Transformers are extremely successful machine learning models whose mathematical properties remain poorly understood. Here, we rigorously characterize the behavior of transformers with hardmax self-attention and normalization sublayers as the number of layers tends to infinity. By viewing such transformers as discrete-time dynamical systems describing the evolution of points in a Euclidean space, and thanks to a geometric interpretation of the self-attention mechanism based on hyperplane separation, we show that the transformer inputs asymptotically converge to a clustered equilibrium determined by special points called \textit{leaders}. We then leverage this theoretical understanding to solve sentiment analysis problems from language processing using a fully interpretable transformer model, which effectively captures `context' by clustering meaningless words around leader words carrying the most meaning. Finally, we outline remaining challenges to bridge the gap between the mathematical analysis of transformers and their real-life implementation.

title: Exploiting the nonzero diagonal pattern in matrix function computations
summary: We consider the task of approximating a matrix function $f(A)$, where $A$ is a matrix in which only a relatively small number of (not necessarily consecutive) sub- and superdiagonals contain nonzero entries. Approximating $f$ by a low-degree polynomial $p$ allows us to obtain sparse approximations to $f(A)$, which one can efficiently work with (while, in general, $f(A)$ is a dense matrix, even when $A$ is sparse). Our approach is based on carefully inspecting the locations where nonzeros can occur in $p(A)$, and identifying the entries in $A$ that influence them. In particular, we illustrate how this approach can be used for efficiently approximating the trace of $f(A)$ and identify how this approach is related to established (stochastic) probing methods for trace estimation. Another application area in which our approach works particularly well is the computation of functions of Toeplitz matrices. Here, studying the sparsity pattern of $p(A)$ allows us to reduce the computation of the whole matrix polynomial to that of a single small-scale submatrix, yielding an algorithm that scales exceptionally well to large problem sizes.

title: AI Simulations Grounded in Rich Self-Reports Increase Accuracy and Reduce Distortion
summary: AI simulations of people built from demographic prompts often misjudge individuals and distort sample-level patterns. We test whether rich self-report data reduce these problems. We developed an AI voice interviewer and conducted two-hour interviews following the American Voices Project protocol with 1,052 U.S. adults, who also completed surveys and behavioral experiments. For each participant, we compared simulations prompted with demographic attributes, self-authored personas, survey responses, interview responses, or combined surveys and interviews. We evaluated accuracy on held-out responses, and measured eight statistical distortions at the sample level: biased averages, compressed variance, distorted response distributions, over-correlated items, attitudes collapsing onto one dimension, ideological sorting, amplified experimental effects, and hyper-rationality. On General Social Survey (GSS) items, demographic simulation led to 60.4% accuracy, whereas interview and survey simulation achieved 69.4% and 69.3%, and combining them reached 72.8%, compared with 79.5% for participants' two-week test-retest agreement. Surveys and interviews also improved prediction of personality traits, but not of incentivized economic choices. Combined interview and survey simulation closed a median of 53.5% of the eight distortion gaps between demographic simulation and participant responses. An open-weight model fine-tuned on other participants' self-reports and responses to the target questions achieved 75.2% GSS accuracy and closed a median of 69.3% of the distortion gap. Overall, both frontier and fine-tuned models reduced distortions without erasing them, but neither reduced hyper-rationality in economic games. These findings demonstrate that qualitative and quantitative self-reports can improve person-specific simulations and reduce statistical distortions.

title: Optimizing Winograd Convolution on ARMv8 processors
summary: As Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) gain increasing prominence in deep learning, algorithms such as Winograd convolution have been introduced to boost computational efficiency. However, existing Winograd implementations often face challenges, including significant transformation overhead, suboptimal computation efficiency, and reduced parallel performance in certain layers. In this work, we present an ARMv8-specific execution framework for Winograd convolution based on a cache-resident, block-wise schedule. By maintaining consecutive memory access where possible and packing data in a customized z-shaped layout, our approach fully exploits a meticulously optimized GEMM micro-kernel that employs a ping-pong technique. Furthermore, we introduce a multidimensional parallelization strategy that selects a thread decomposition across the batch, tile, input-channel, and output-channel loops according to layer shape and coordinates the resulting thread groups with the fused block-wise execution schedule. To further boost performance, we manually optimize each micro-kernel in AArch64 assembly, carefully tuning blocking parameters for the ARMv8 architecture to minimize transformation overhead and maximize computational throughput. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves up to $4.74\times$, $4.10\times$, $4.72\times$, and $10.57\times$ speedups over NCNN, NNPACK, FastConv, and ACL, respectively, on the Kunpeng 920 platform when using multiple threads, with corresponding gains of $5.46\times$, $2.81\times$, $6.11\times$, and $8.05\times$ on the AWS Graviton2, and $3.32\times$, $3.68\times$, $5.84\times$, and $9.28\times$ on the Phytium 2000+.

title: NS-Gym: A Comprehensive and Open-Source Simulation Framework for Non-Stationary Markov Decision Processes
comments: NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track. 34 pages, 26 figures, 20 tables
summary: Many real-world applications require decision-making where the environmental dynamics evolve over time. These non-stationary environments pose significant challenges to traditional decision-making models, which typically assume stationary dynamics. Non-stationary Markov decision processes (NS-MDPs) offer a framework to model and solve decision problems under such changing conditions. However, there are no standardized simulation frameworks for NS-MDPs, as opposed to widely popular frameworks for stationary problems. We present NS-Gym, the first simulation toolkit designed explicitly for NS-MDPs, integrated within the popular Gymnasium framework. In NS-Gym, we segregate the evolution of the environmental parameters that characterize non-stationarity from the agent's decision-making module, allowing for modular and flexible adaptations to dynamic environments. We review prior work in this domain and present a toolkit encapsulating key problem characteristics and types in NS-MDPs. This toolkit is the first effort to develop a set of standardized interfaces and benchmark problems to enable consistent and reproducible evaluation of algorithms under non-stationary conditions. We also benchmark several algorithmic approaches from prior work on NS-MDPs using NS-Gym. We envision that NS-Gym will enable researchers to study decision-making under non-stationarity by providing standardized interfaces, simulation frameworks, and benchmark problems. Project documentation, webpage, and code can be found at https://nsgym.io and https://github.com/scope-lab-vu/ns_gym

title: Exact Sequence Interpolation with Transformers
comments: Funded by the European Union's HORIZON-MSCA-2021-DN-01-01, through the ModConFlex project ("Modelling and control of flexible structures interacting with fluids"; Grant Agreement No. 101073558; DOI: https://doi.org/10.3030/101073558). Accompanying code available at: https://github.com/DCN-FAU-AvH/exactInterpTF, code DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21107925
summary: We prove that transformers can exactly interpolate datasets of finite input sequences in $\mathbb{R}^d$, $d\geq 2$, with corresponding output sequences of smaller or equal length. Specifically, given $N$ sequences of arbitrary but finite lengths in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and output sequences of lengths $m^1, \dots, m^N \in \mathbb{N}$, we construct a transformer with $\mathcal{O}(\sum_{j=1}^N m^j)$ blocks and $\smash{\mathcal{O}(d \sum_{j=1}^N m^j)}$ parameters that exactly interpolates the dataset. Our construction provides complexity estimates that are independent of the input sequence length, by alternating feed-forward and self-attention layers and by capitalizing on the clustering effect inherent to the latter. Our novel constructive method also uses low-rank parameter matrices in the self-attention mechanism, a common feature of practical transformer implementations. These results are first established in the hardmax self-attention setting, where the geometric structure permits an explicit and quantitative analysis, and are then extended to the softmax setting. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of our exact interpolation construction to learning problems, in particular by providing convergence guarantees to a global minimizer under regularized training strategies. Our analysis contributes to the theoretical understanding of transformer models, offering an explanation for their excellent performance in exact sequence-to-sequence interpolation tasks.

title: RustMC: Automated Verification of Real-World Concurrent Rust
summary: RustMC is a stateless model checker that targets push-button verification of unmodified concurrent Rust programs. As both Rust and C/C++ compile to LLVM IR, RustMC builds on GenMC which provides a verification framework for LLVM IR. This allows verification of Rust code and any foreign function dependencies. In this tool paper we present key implementation challenges, use-cases, and an empirical evaluation of RustMC. The challenges include intercepting threading operations, promoting memory intrinsics, and handling uninitialised accesses, all stemming from Rust's unique compilation strategy. Case studies adapted from real-world programs show RustMC finds concurrency bugs in unsafe Rust code, FFI calls to C/C++, and atomic operations. We evaluate our tool's functionality on the Loom model checker test suite and a set of production-level Rust concurrent data structures.

title: SiGMA: Learning under Graph-Level Heterogeneity with Gated Message-Passing and Attention
summary: In graph-level learning, graph neural networks are typically applied with a fixed computational template: the same depth, local message-passing operator, and global attention mechanism are used for every input graph. However, different graphs within the same dataset can vary substantially in prediction difficulty and may require different mixtures of local and non-local computation. We study this phenomenon as graph-level heterogeneity in both classification and regression tasks. To address it, we propose SiGMA (Sigmoid Gated Message-Passing and Attention), a gated hybrid graph neural network architecture that combines message-passing and attention heads within each layer. Inspired by the growing use of gated attention and gated computation in large language models and vision transformers, each head in SiGMA is modulated by a learned node-wise sigmoid gate, allowing the model to adaptively regulate which local or global mechanisms are active for different nodes, layers, and input graphs. The resulting architecture can emulate expressive message-passing backbones, admits near-identity computation paths that are not forced to over-smooth, and enables direct non-local communication beyond message-passing neighborhoods to mitigate over-squashing. Empirically, SiGMA achieves strong performance across graph-level benchmarks, consistently matching or improving over competitive graph transformer and hybrid baselines. Our results suggest that adapting computation to graph-level heterogeneity is a promising direction for building more flexible and effective graph learning architectures.

title: Low-regularity error estimates of a filtered Lie-Trotter splitting scheme for the Zakharov system in arbitrary dimensions
summary: We establish low-regularity error estimates for a fully discrete, filtered Lie--Trotter splitting scheme for the Zakharov system on the $d$-dimensional torus. Our analysis relies on multilinear estimates in discrete Bourgain spaces. Specifically, for an exact solution $(E,z,z_t)$ with regularity $H^{s+r+1/2}\times H^{s+r}\times H^{s+r-1}$ on a fixed time interval, we prove an error bound of order $\mathcal{O}(τ^{s/2}+N^{-s})$ in $H^{r+1/2}\times H^r\times H^{r-1}$ for $s\in(0,2]$, where $r=\max\{0,\tfrac d2-1\}$, $τ$ is the time step, and $N$ is the number of spatial grid points in each coordinate direction. The analysis treats the coupled nonlinearities directly, without introducing the time-differentiated auxiliary variables of an Ozawa-type transformation. Under the stated CFL condition, which renders the filter inactive on the Fourier collocation space, the scheme preserves discrete mass exactly in exact arithmetic. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical convergence rates and show small relative energy errors over the tested time intervals.

title: Exploring Explainable Multi-agent MCTS-minimax Hybrids in Board Game Using Process Mining
summary: Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is a family of sampling-based search algorithms widely used for online planning in sequential decision-making domains and at the heart of many recent advances in artificial intelligence. Understanding the behavior of MCTS agents is difficult for developers and users due to the frequently large and complex search trees that result from the simulation of many possible futures, their evaluations, and their relationships. This paper presents our ongoing investigation into potential explanations for the decision-making and behavior of MCTS. A weakness of MCTS is that it constructs a highly selective tree and, as a result, can miss crucial moves and fall into tactical traps. Full-width minimax search constitutes the solution. We integrate shallow minimax search into the rollout phase of multi-agent MCTS and use process mining technique to explain agents' strategies in 3v3 checkers.

title: Adaptive Finite State Projection with Quantile-Based Pruning for Solving the Chemical Master Equation
summary: We present an adaptive Finite State Projection (FSP) method for efficiently solving the Chemical Master Equation (CME) with rigorous error control. Our approach integrates time-stepping with dynamic state-space truncation, balancing accuracy and computational cost. Krylov subspace methods approximate the matrix exponential, while quantile-based pruning controls state-space growth by removing low-probability states. Theoretical error bounds ensure that the truncation error remains bounded by the pruned mass at each step, which is user-controlled, and does not propagate forward in time. Numerical experiments on biochemical systems, including the Lotka-Volterra and Michaelis-Menten and bi-stable toggle switch models.

title: Say It Another Way: Auditing LLMs with a User-Grounded Automated Paraphrasing Framework
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are highly sensitive to subtle changes in prompt phrasing, posing challenges for reliable auditing. Prior methods often apply unconstrained prompt paraphrasing, which risk missing linguistic and demographic factors that shape authentic user interactions. We introduce AUGMENT (Automated User-Grounded Modeling and Evaluation of Natural Language Transformations), a framework for generating controlled paraphrases, grounded in user behaviors. AUGMENT leverages linguistically informed rules and enforces quality through checks on instruction adherence, semantic similarity, and realism, ensuring paraphrases are both reliable and meaningful for auditing. Through case studies on the BBQ and MMLU datasets, we show that controlled paraphrases uncover systematic weaknesses that remain obscured under unconstrained variation. These results highlight the value of the AUGMENT framework for reliable auditing.

title: HOPSE: Scalable Higher-Order Positional and Structural Encoder for Combinatorial Representations
summary: While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective at modeling relational data, pairwise connections cannot fully capture multi-way relationships naturally present in complex real-world systems. In response to this, Topological Deep Learning (TDL) leverages more general combinatorial representations--such as simplicial or cellular complexes--to accommodate higher-order interactions. Existing TDL methods often extend GNNs through Higher-Order Message Passing (HOMP), but face critical scalability challenges due to the steep complexity overhead of propagating messages through combinatorial structures. To overcome this limitation, we propose HOPSE (Higher-Order Positional and Structural Encoder), a framework free of learnable message passing layers that uses Hasse graph decompositions to derive efficient and expressive encodings over arbitrary higher-order domains. Notably, HOPSE training and inference scale linearly with the size of combinatorial representations while preserving the expressive power and permutation equivariance of the HOMP approaches. Experiments on molecular and topological benchmarks show that it matches or surpasses state-of-the-art performance while consistently achieving speedups over HOMP-based models, opening a new path for scalable TDL. The code is available at https://github.com/geometric-intelligence/topobench.

title: Human-AI Writing as Distributed Cognition: Reassessing Collaborative Writing Theories in the Age of LLMs
summary: In this paper, we conduct a structured synthesis of existing theories and frameworks on human-human collaborative writing to assess how co-writing with AI reshapes writing in knowledge work settings, and draw seven insights along with design implications for human-AI collaborative writing tools. Our main argument is that, as we delegate more writing to AI, our cognitive process shifts from the traditional plan/write/review process to a plan/delegate/review process, reshaping the distribution of the cognitive labor between human writers and AI writing tools. To ensure that humans cognitively stay in the loop, we discuss a ``prototyping'' approach, where the writing tool scaffolds a healthier distribution of cognition through rapid, small-scale iterations that keep writers mentally in the loop even when generation is delegated to AI. We aim to bring theoretical grounding and practical guidance to the interaction designs of human-AI collaborative writing, with the goal of balancing automation with cognitive integrity.

title: Human-like Semantic Navigation for Autonomous Driving using Knowledge Representation and Large Language Models
summary: Achieving full automation in self-driving vehicles remains a challenge, especially in dynamic urban environments where navigation requires real-time adaptability. Existing systems struggle to handle navigation plans when faced with unpredictable changes in road layouts, spontaneous detours, or missing map data, due to their heavy reliance on predefined cartographic information. In this work, we explore the use of Large Language Models to generate Answer Set Programming rules by translating informal navigation instructions into structured, logic-based reasoning. ASP provides non-monotonic reasoning, allowing autonomous vehicles to adapt to evolving scenarios without relying on predefined maps. We present an experimental evaluation in which LLMs generate ASP constraints that encode real-world urban driving logic into a formal knowledge representation. By automating the translation of informal navigation instructions into logical rules, our method improves adaptability and explainability in autonomous navigation. Results show that LLM-driven ASP rule generation supports semantic-based decision-making, offering an explainable framework for dynamic navigation planning that aligns closely with how humans communicate navigational intent.

title: Finite element spaces of double forms
summary: The tensor product of two differential forms of degree $p$ and $q$ is a multilinear form that is alternating in its first $p$ arguments and alternating in its last $q$ arguments. These forms, which are known as double forms or $(p,q)$-forms, play a central role in certain differential complexes that arise when studying partial differential equations. We construct piecewise polynomial finite element spaces for all of the natural subspaces of the space of $(p,q)$-forms, excluding one subspace which fails to admit a piecewise constant discretization. As special cases, our construction recovers known finite element spaces for symmetric matrices with tangential-tangential continuity (the Regge finite elements), symmetric matrices with normal-normal continuity, and trace-free matrices with normal-tangential continuity. It also gives rise to new spaces, like a finite element space for tensors possessing the symmetries of the Riemann curvature tensor.

title: RTime-QA: A Benchmark for Atomic Temporal Event Understanding in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) perform well on video benchmarks, yet many video questions can be answered from a single frame or from language priors, which leaves open whether these models perceive how an event unfolds in time. We introduce \rtqa, a benchmark for atomic temporal event understanding built on time-reversed question pairs: each video is accompanied by its reversal, and each question is asked on both videos with identical text and options but different correct answers, so that a deterministic model that ignores the order of the frames cannot answer both. \rtqa{} comprises 8,420 questions of five types on 1,278 videos, 639 videos and their reversals. The questions are derived from event annotations that a proposer model writes, a reviewer model checks and human annotators verify, and three subsets target fast evaluation (\rtqatiny), questions that are hard to answer from the first and last frames (\rtqacore) and two consecutive events (\rtqacomp). All 20 evaluated models are less accurate on reversed videos. On \rtqafull, proprietary models answer both questions of 90.6--94.4\% of the pairs and the strongest open-source model of 66.8\%; on \rtqacore, the proprietary models drop to 55.6--64.5\%, and shuffling the frames reduces the paired accuracy of the tested open-source models to 3.4--7.4\%. We further build \rtqatrain{} with the same pipeline, without human verification, and train three open-source MLLMs on it with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (DAPO) under matched settings: both raise paired accuracy on \rtqafull, SFT by 20.7--27.4 points and DAPO by 5.9--22.9 points. For Qwen3.5-9B-Thinking, the training data also help on two other temporal benchmarks: SFT and DAPO raise the Vinoground text score by 5.8 and 3.8 points, respectively, and DAPO raises the TVBench macro accuracy by 4.6 points.

title: Morphology-driven single-domain generalization for cross-cohort Alzheimer's disease detection using 3D MRIs
summary: Although Alzheimer's disease detection via MRIs has advanced significantly thanks to contemporary deep learning models, challenges such as class imbalance, protocol variations, and limited dataset diversity often hinder their generalization capacity. To address this issue, this article focuses on the single domain generalization setting, where given the data of one domain, a model is designed and developed with maximal performance w.r.t. an unseen domain of distinct distribution. Since brain morphology is known to play a crucial role in Alzheimer's diagnosis, we propose the use of learnable pseudo-morphological modules aimed at producing shape-aware, anatomically meaningful class-specific augmentations in combination with a supervised contrastive learning module to extract robust class-specific representations. Experiments conducted across three datasets show improved performance and generalization capacity, especially under class imbalance and imaging protocol variations. The source code will be made available upon acceptance at https://github.com/zobia111/SDG-Alzheimer.

title: Evaluating and Mitigating Skin Color Bias in Skin Lesion Classificatio
summary: Skin lesion classifiers may overlook performance disparity because of subtle skin tone variations by treating skin tone as a categorical attribute. This study proposes a method that represents skin tone as a continuous attribute and assigns individual weights to each sample based on its nonlinear relationship with classification performance. Evaluations on two dermatological datasets showed that fairness metrics were sensitive to skin-color categorization. The proposed method also demonstrated more stable fairness improvements than conventional categorical reweighting while generally preserving classification performance.

title: Recursive Learning-Based Virtual Buffering for Analytical Global Placement
summary: Due to the skewed scaling of interconnect versus cell delay in modern technology nodes, placement with buffer porosity (i.e., cell density) awareness is essential for timing closure in physical synthesis flows. However, existing approaches face two key challenges: (i) traditional van Ginneken-Lillis-style buffering approaches are computationally expensive during global placement; and (ii) machine learning-based approaches, such as BufFormer, lack a thorough consideration of Electrical Rule Check (ERC) violations and fail to "close the loop" back into the physical design flow. In this work, we propose MLBuf-RePlAce, the first open-source learning-driven virtual buffering-aware analytical global placement framework, built on top of the OpenROAD infrastructure. MLBuf-RePlAce adopts an efficient recursive learning-based generative buffering approach to predict buffer types and locations, addressing ERC violations during global placement. We compare MLBuf-RePlAce against the default virtual buffering-based timing-driven global placer in OpenROAD, using open-source testcases from the TILOS MacroPlacement and OpenROAD-flow-scripts repositories. Without degradation of post-route power, MLBuf-RePlAce achieves (maximum, average) improvements of (56%, 31%) in total negative slack (TNS) within the open-source OpenROAD flow. When evaluated by completion in a commercial flow, MLBuf-RePlAce achieves (maximum, average) improvements of (53%, 28%) in TNS with an average of 0.2% improvement in post-route power.

title: HE-LRM: Encrypted Deep Learning Recommendation Models using Fully Homomorphic Encryption
comments: 16 pages, 12 figures, 2 tables. Akshath Mahajan and Karthik Garimella contributed equally
summary: FHE inference systems primarily target models with dense inputs, while Deep Learning Recommendation Models (DLRMs) contain sparse categorical features that require lookups into embedding tables. Encrypted lookups are challenging because indexing is not natively supported and must be expressed using SIMD arithmetic. A direct one-hot formulation does not scale. Prior work addresses parts of this problem through embedding compression or compact encrypted queries. However, it does not address complete DLRM inference, leaving open how private lookup interacts with downstream computation and memory constraints. We present HE-LRM, the first end-to-end FHE system for private DLRM inference. We use deterministic compositional embedding compression with client-side digit decomposition, avoiding expensive homomorphic selector construction while consuming only one multiplicative level. We further develop a block-diagonal packing strategy that performs lookups across multiple embedding tables using optimized BSGS linear transformations and produces encrypted embeddings directly compatible with downstream inference. We extend Orion with a high-performance GPU backend and achieve 9 ms for single-inference embedding lookup. We also show that GPU memory capacity limits batching and therefore the latency-bound throughput in such systems. On Criteo, HE-LRM achieves complete encrypted inference with server-side latencies of 154-247 ms on a single GPU. We open-source HE-LRM at https://github.com/baahl-nyu/orion
comment: 16 pages, 12 figures, 2 tables. Akshath Mahajan and Karthik Garimella contributed equally

title: Visual Contextual Attack: Jailbreaking MLLMs with Image-Driven Context Injection
summary: With the emergence of strong vision language capabilities, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated tremendous potential for real-world applications. However, the security vulnerabilities exhibited by the visual modality pose significant challenges to deploying such models in open-world environments. Recent studies have successfully induced harmful responses from target MLLMs by encoding harmful textual semantics directly into visual inputs. However, in these approaches, the visual modality primarily serves as a trigger for unsafe behavior, often exhibiting semantic ambiguity and lacking grounding in realistic scenarios. In this work, we define a novel setting: vision-centric jailbreak, where visual information serves as a necessary component in constructing a complete and realistic jailbreak context. Building on this setting, we propose the VisCo (Visual Contextual) Attack. VisCo fabricates contextual dialogue using four distinct vision-focused strategies, dynamically generating auxiliary images when necessary to construct a vision-centric jailbreak scenario. To maximize attack effectiveness, it incorporates automatic toxicity obfuscation and semantic refinement to produce a final attack prompt that reliably triggers harmful responses from the target black-box MLLMs. Specifically, VisCo achieves a toxicity score of 4.78 and an Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 85% on MM-SafetyBench against GPT-4o, significantly outperforming the baseline, which achieves a toxicity score of 2.48 and an ASR of 22.2%. Code: https://github.com/Dtc7w3PQ/Visco-Attack.

title: Response Attack: Exploiting Contextual Priming to Jailbreak Large Language Models
comments: 20 pages, 10 figures. Code and data available at https://github.com/Dtc7w3PQ/Response-Attack
summary: Contextual priming, where earlier stimuli covertly bias later judgments, offers an unexplored attack surface for large language models (LLMs). We uncover a contextual priming vulnerability in which the previous response in the dialogue can steer its subsequent behavior toward policy-violating content. While existing jailbreak attacks largely rely on single-turn or multi-turn prompt manipulations, or inject static in-context examples, these methods suffer from limited effectiveness, inefficiency, or semantic drift. We introduce Response Attack (RA), a novel framework that strategically leverages intermediate, mildly harmful responses as contextual primers within a dialogue. By reformulating harmful queries and injecting these intermediate responses before issuing a targeted trigger prompt, RA exploits a previously overlooked vulnerability in LLMs. Extensive experiments across eight state-of-the-art LLMs show that RA consistently achieves significantly higher attack success rates than nine leading jailbreak baselines. Our results demonstrate that the success of RA is directly attributable to the strategic use of intermediate responses, which induce models to generate more explicit and relevant harmful content while maintaining stealth, efficiency, and fidelity to the original query. The code and data are available at https://github.com/Dtc7w3PQ/Response-Attack.
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures. Code and data available at https://github.com/Dtc7w3PQ/Response-Attack

title: Mix-Opt: Mixed Optimization for Memory-Efficient Personalization of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
comments: Extended version accepted to NeurIPS 2026. The earlier 4-page version received the Best Paper Award at the ICCV 2025 LIMIT Workshop
summary: Memory-efficient personalization is essential for adapting text-to-image diffusion models while preserving user privacy and operating within the limited computational resources of edge devices. To this end, we propose Mix-Opt, a novel mixed optimization framework that adaptively chooses between backpropagation on low-resolution images (BP-low) and zeroth-order optimization on high-resolution images (ZO-high), guided by the characteristics of the diffusion process. As observed in our experiments, BP-low efficiently adapts the model to target-specific features but suffers from structural distortions due to resolution mismatch. Conversely, ZO-high refines high-resolution details with minimal memory overhead but faces slow convergence when applied without prior adaptation. By complementing both methods, our framework leverages BP-low for effective personalization while using ZO-high to maintain structural consistency, achieving memory-efficient and high-quality fine-tuning. To maximize the efficacy of both BP-low and ZO-high, we introduce a timestep-aware probabilistic function that dynamically selects the appropriate optimization strategy during training. This function mitigates overfitting from BP-low at high timesteps, where structural information is critical, while ensuring that ZO-high is applied more effectively as training progresses. Experimental results across both U-Net- and DiT-based diffusion models demonstrate that Mix-Opt achieves competitive personalization performance while significantly reducing memory consumption. Mix-Opt enables scalable, high-quality personalization without modifying the inference process or increasing inference latency.
comment: Extended version accepted to NeurIPS 2026. The earlier 4-page version received the Best Paper Award at the ICCV 2025 LIMIT Workshop

title: A Black-Box Approach for Exogenous Replenishment in Online Resource Allocation
summary: In a typical online resource allocation problem, we start with a fixed inventory of resources and make online allocation decisions in response to resource requests that arrive sequentially over a finite horizon. We consider settings where the inventory is replenished over time according to an unknown exogenous process. We introduce black-box methods that extend any existing algorithm, originally designed without considering replenishment, into one that works with an arbitrary (adversarial or stochastic) replenishment process. Our approach preserves the original algorithm's competitive ratio in regimes with large initial inventory, thereby enabling the seamless integration of exogenous replenishment into a large body of existing algorithmic results for both adversarial and stochastic arrival models.

title: Training Self-Supervised Depth Completion Using Sparse Measurements and a Single Image
comments: The writing is very poor, the methodology not great, and the experiments not well conducted
summary: Depth completion is an important vision task, and many efforts have been made to enhance the quality of depth maps from sparse depth measurements. Despite significant advances, training these models to recover dense depth from sparse measurements remains a challenging problem. Supervised learning methods rely on dense depth labels to predict unobserved regions, while self-supervised approaches require image sequences to enforce geometric constraints and photometric consistency between frames. However, acquiring dense annotations is costly, and multi-frame dependencies limit the applicability of self-supervised methods in static or single-frame scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose a novel self-supervised depth completion paradigm that requires only sparse depth measurements and their corresponding image for training. Unlike existing methods, our approach eliminates the need for dense depth labels or additional images captured from neighboring viewpoints. By leveraging the characteristics of depth distribution, we design novel loss functions that effectively propagate depth information from observed points to unobserved regions. Additionally, we incorporate segmentation maps generated by vision foundation models to further enhance depth estimation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

title: Frames over finite fields with respect to the Galois inner product and their connections to self-orthogonal and LCD codes
summary: In this paper, we generalize the theory of frames to vector spaces over finite fields equipped with the $\ell$-Galois inner product. We introduce $\ell$-Galois analogues of fundamental concepts in frame theory and investigate extensions of existing results to the $\ell$-Galois setting. In particular, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for a given matrix to be the $\ell$-Galois Gram matrix of a frame and show that such frames are unique up to isometry. We also extend Gerzon's bound to $\ell$-Galois equiangular systems and show that equality in this bound yields an $\ell$-Galois equiangular tight frame. Furthermore, we investigate the connections between $\ell$-Galois frames and $\ell$-Galois self-orthogonal and LCD codes over finite fields. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for constructing $\ell$-Galois equiangular tight frames from self-dual codes, generalizing existing results by Shi et al. on the relationship between frames and self-dual codes over finite fields. Beyond self-dual codes, we provide sufficient conditions for constructing $\ell$-Galois equiangular tight frames from linear codes using their automorphism groups, together with explicit examples.

title: Building verifiable databases at scale from the chemical literature via a multi-agent system
comments: v4: substantially revised; new title, one added author. Adds a expanded 424-graphic benchmark, generalist-agent baselines, calibrated confidence scores, and downstream tasks: condition ranking and product prediction trained on a 60,103-reaction photochemistry database. Results in v1-v3 are superseded. 92 pages, 5 figures
summary: Accelerating chemical research with artificial intelligence requires high-quality databases. However, many reactions exist only as graphics drawn for human readers, which machines must read exactly. Specialist software is precise but rigid, whereas multimodal language models are flexible yet often write incorrect structures; neither flags errors. We present ChemEAGLE, a multi-agent system where tools supply structures and a language model extends their reach through judgments that programs apply. On 424 published graphics, its F1 score for exactly correct reactions was 82.2%, against 47.7% for a tool-equipped generalist agent, and calibrated confidence limited review to 35% of reactions at 96.6% accuracy. Without review, it built a 60,103-reaction photochemistry database whose records trained models to rank conditions and predict products. Verifiable databases can thus be built at scale.

Adds a expanded 424-graphic benchmark, generalist-agent baselines, calibrated confidence scores, and downstream tasks: condition ranking and product prediction trained on a 60,103-reaction photochemistry database. Results in v1-v3 are superseded. 92 pages, 5 figures

title: DualTopo: Spatio-Temporal Lane Graph Generation with Dual Latent World Models and Parallel Query Supervision
comments: The manuscript has been extensively rewritten and reorganized, and the title has been updated. The revised version retains the core method of the old one
summary: Lane topology reasoning constructs a spatiotemporal road graph G = (V, E) in bird's-eye view (BEV), providing structured road representations for planning-oriented autonomous driving. Stream-based methods propagate temporal cues at both the query and BEV levels, yet suffer from two critical limitations: (1) initialized queries receive insufficient supervision, as temporal queries dominate Hungarian matching and leave them undertrained; and (2) temporal propagation is weakened by BEV boundary information loss during feature warping. Since initialized queries serve as propagation anchors, particularly at the first frame, these deficiencies compound across frames and degrade graph generation quality. We propose DualTopo, a spatio-temporal lane graph generation framework with dual latent world models and dual parallel decoder pathways. The dual-pathway decoder supervises temporal and initialized queries concurrently, ensuring initialized queries are well-trained and serve as reliable anchors. Dual latent world models conditioned on ego-motion propagate latent state representations from past observations to the present, substantially improving spatiotemporal graph generation. Extensive experiments on OpenLane-V2 demonstrate leading lane detection accuracy and competitive topology graph prediction. Code is available at https://github.com/YimingYang23/DualTopo.

title: TAR: Temporal Anchor-Constrained Reasoning for Video Temporal Grounding
summary: Video Temporal Grounding (VTG) aims to localize specific video segments corresponding to natural language queries. While recent Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) employ Reinforcement Learning to generate Chains-of-Thought (CoT), they typically rely solely on outcome-based supervision. Consequently, this often leads to hallucinations, where the reasoning process becomes disconnected from the visual content and the final prediction. Existing attempts to mitigate this by relying on external supervision from larger models or separate reward models are computationally expensive and prone to rigid patterns. To address these challenges, we propose TAR (Temporal Anchor-Constrained Reasoning), a framework that introduces the temporal anchor (T-anchor) as a transparent and auditable checkpoint mechanism. T-anchor enforces progressive refinement within the CoT, compelling the model to continuously ground its intermediate thoughts in visual evidence and iteratively calibrate temporal predictions, thereby significantly enhancing the faithfulness and autonomy of the reasoning process and final accuracy. Furthermore, we introduce a bootstrapping paradigm that automatically harvests high-quality CoT data using only a standard 7B model, eliminating the dependency on ultra-large models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TAR achieves state-of-the-art performance and generates faithful, autonomous, and progressively refined reasoning traces.

title: Humans and AI respond similarly to task difficulty when reasoning about content moderation dilemmas
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) generate intermediate reasoning steps before producing answers, improving performance on challenging problems by iteratively developing solutions. There is evidence that LRMs expend more effort on the problems that take people longer to solve, but it is unclear whether these relationships hold on more subjective tasks without verifiable answers. This study addresses this issue through an experiment using a content moderation task, where task difficulty is manipulated by varying the relative offensiveness of two different options. Comparing six large reasoning models with 1,854 human subjects, we find that models expend more reasoning effort, measured using the length of the chain-of-thought (CoT), on the kinds of cases that take people longer to adjudicate. People took 31\% longer and models produced 51 to 306\% longer CoTs when offensiveness was held constant across the two posts. The correlation is relatively low for individual decisions ($r = 0.15$--$0.19$), but average response times and average reasoning effort are closely correlated when tasks are grouped by the types of offensive language ($r = 0.85$--$0.93$). Qualitative analyses of the CoT summaries from Gemini 2.5 Pro corroborate these findings, showing that secondary factors were mentioned more often when offensiveness was fixed. The results point to the potential for using reasoning traces to prioritize difficult cases and enhance interpretability.

title: NewsReX: An Open-Source Multi-Framework for Neural News Recommendation
comments: 5 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at CIKM 2026 (Resource Track), Rome, Italy. Code: https://github.com/igor17400/NewsReX
summary: Reproducing and comparing results in neural news recommendation research remains difficult due to fragmented codebases, inconsistent preprocessing pipelines, and tight coupling between models and deep learning frameworks. We present NewsReX, an open-source framework that unifies multiple neural news recommendation models across two ML backends (PyTorch and JAX/Flax). Models are defined through a structured YAML specification that captures architecture, training recipe, and data contract, decoupling model definition from framework-specific implementation. A Hydra-based configuration system enables composable experiments with single-command framework switching. We provide cross-framework parity tests to verify numerical consistency across backends, allowing researchers to reproduce results from the original implementations and then transfer experiments to their preferred framework. We report comprehensive experiments on the MIND-small benchmark with multiple seeds per model and per framework, and demonstrate multilingual generalization by training on a proprietary Japanese news dataset from Nikkei News. We also publish pre-trained model weights on Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/newsrex) so that researchers can build on existing results without redundant retraining, reducing both computational cost and energy consumption. All source code, experiment configurations, and trained model weights are publicly available.
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at CIKM 2026 (Resource Track), Rome, Italy. Code: https://github.com/igor17400/NewsReX

title: AutoPBO: LLM-powered Optimization for Local Search PBO Solvers
comments: Author order updated. No changes to the scientific content
summary: Pseudo-Boolean Optimization (PBO) provides a powerful framework for modeling combinatorial problems through pseudo-Boolean (PB) constraints. Local search solvers have shown excellent performance in PBO solving, and their efficiency is highly dependent on their internal heuristics to guide the search. Still, their design often requires significant expert effort and manual tuning in practice. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential in automating algorithm design, their application to optimizing PBO solvers remains unexplored. In this work, we introduce AutoPBO, a novel LLM-powered framework to automatically enhance PBO local search solvers. We conduct experiments on a broad range of four public benchmarks, including one real-world benchmark, a benchmark from PB competition, an integer linear programming optimization benchmark, and a crafted combinatorial benchmark, to evaluate the performance improvement achieved by AutoPBO and compare it with six state-of-the-art competitors, including two local search PBO solvers NuPBO and OraSLS, two complete PB solvers PBO-IHS and RoundingSat, and two mixed integer programming (MIP) solvers Gurobi and SCIP. AutoPBO demonstrates significant improvements over previous local search approaches, while maintaining competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art competitors. The results suggest that AutoPBO offers a promising approach to automating local search solver design.
