title: Why ML-based cough models do not generalize: a systematic cross-dataset evaluation for tuberculosis screening
summary: Cough acoustics are promising for non-invasive tuberculosis (TB) screening, yet whether machine learning (ML) models capture disease-related acoustics or artifacts of data collection remains unresolved. We evaluated the cross-dataset generalizability of classical ML and deep learning (DL) cough-based TB classifiers across three independent datasets. Despite moderate within-dataset performance (ROC-AUC up to $0.76 \pm 0.06$), both pipelines fail to generalize, with external performance frequently below 0.6, indicating a possible limitation of the data. We further observed that audio representations are organized by recording device and dataset rather than TB status, predicted TB probability tracks country-level prevalence in CODA, and device mismatch degrades transfer while device-diverse training improves it. Additionally, a clinical-variable baseline generalizes more consistently (ROC-AUC $0.65-0.71$), indicating acquisition-specific variability in acoustics is a stronger driver of poor generalizability. High within-dataset performance is not enough. External validation is essential before cough-based TB models are clinically ready.

title: Towards Efficient Auto-Interpretability of Boltz-1 Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) could turn AI models in Biology and other fields into engines of scientific discovery by explaining the superhuman capabilities of those models. We postulate that a latent is useful if we know three things: whether it is coherent, whether it can be described, and whether that description has predictive power. These questions are routinely conflated. We assemble them into a single pipeline and report some practical innovations. First, cross-seed dictionary stability prioritises which latents are worth spending resources to investigate. Second, an intruder-detection task asks whether a latent's activating examples share a recognizable pattern. Third, a separate pass proposes a candidate biological description which we convert into falsifiable predictions which can be tested in silico. Deployed on the Boltz-1 Pairformer trunk, stability prioritisation finds interpretable latents using about 4.4 times fewer latent evaluations each, and at 5.2 times lower measured LLM cost, while recovering over half of them. However, we notice that in our setup the LLM judge is heavily biased towards consistent residue identity and a simple filter that selects for features with high amino-acid identity precision outperforms the stability thresholding. This simpler method has the added benefit of requiring no extra SAE seeds but it remains uncertain if it reflects a genuinely useful heuristic or an limitation of the LLM judge.

title: Representation Learning with Quantum Signal Processing
comments: 7 pages, 2 figures (including End Matter); 16-page Supplemental Material with 1 figure. v2 improved presentation and expanded proof details in the Supplemental Material
summary: Representation learning begins when training changes the features that define similarity between data. A frozen-kernel model only reweights a fixed geometry. We establish quantum signal processing (QSP) as a solvable quantum model of the representation-learning regime. At arbitrary depth, we compute the exact mean and variance of its quantum neural tangent kernel, revealing an input-dependent angular geometry whose diagonal remains non-self-averaging even when the underlying unitary approaches Haar randomness. We also prove a sparse-data guarantee for the full nonlinear gradient flow without freezing or ensemble-averaging the kernel: the realized dynamics converges to an integrable scalar flow with a time-dependent kernel closure and explicit convergence times. A finite-depth speed limit holds for every data set and trajectory. At higher data density, numerical results show coupled evolution beyond both the scalar and frozen-kernel descriptions. These results give a controlled theory of learned quantum data geometry with provable training dynamics beyond the frozen limit.
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures (including End Matter); 16-page Supplemental Material with 1 figure. v2 improved presentation and expanded proof details in the Supplemental Material

title: BEAM3R: Beam's-eye-view architecture with Mamba-3 for implicit dose reconstruction
summary: To enable accurate and rapid photon control point and proton beamlet dose calculation in the DoseRAD2026 challenge, we present BEAM3R, a dose estimation framework operating in beam's-eye-view (BEV). Our core innovation combines a Mamba-3 state-space depth-sequence core with physics-based transport conditioning to model long-range depth transport without expensive 3D convolutions. BEAM3R shares a 2D CNN encoder-decoder architecture for photon and proton dose tasks, processing per-plane BEV slices. Proton beamlets are conditioned on water equivalent thickness and remaining range, encoding the parameters determining Bragg peak position. Photon models use a bidirectional Mamba-3 core to capture dose contributions from materials downstream of the calculation point, while the proton model uses a forward core with learned energy-prefix tokens and a Bragg-peak refinement module. To reduce interpolation artifacts and support high spatial resolution, we introduce axial grid alignment of BEV lattices with CT slices and an implicit super-resolution representation arranged as channels, evaluated by a differentiable Triton-accelerated resampler that reconstructs packed cubic B-spline coefficients directly in CT space. For MRI-based tasks, synthetic CTs (sCT) are generated using a conditional GAN with a SwinUNETR generator and a PatchGAN discriminator. On the preliminary DoseRAD2026 test set, CT-to-photon and CT-to-proton models achieved 1%/1 mm local gamma pass rates of 96.8% and 96.0%, with stratified plan-level MAEs of 0.0041 and 0.0079. Substituting sCT reduced gamma pass rates to 89.7% for photon and 75.4% proton plan level doses, with stratified plan-level MAEs of 0.0093 and 0.0336. Standardised runtimes were 23.4 s and 18.4 s for CT-to-photon and CT-to-proton prediction, increasing to 39.7 s and 42.8 s for the corresponding MRI-based pipelines.

title: Direct Numerical Simulation of Thermoacoustically Unstable Flames Via Non-Drifting Acoustic Delay Characteristic Boundary Conditions
summary: In this work, Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) of thermoacoustically unstable free flames in closed-open tubes are presented. Simulations demonstrate nonlinear saturation of the primary instability as the flame flattens, resulting in a quasiperiodic acoustic limit cycle. Acoustic forcing is used to trigger secondary parametric instability, causing an oscillatory flame fingering characteristic of the unsteady Rayleigh-Taylor effect. To reduce computational cost, we perform DNS only on the region surrounding the flame. Acoustics at in- and outflows are described using the Navier-Stokes Characteristic Boundary Condition (NSCBC) method to model their delayed reentry into the domain in a formulation referred to as the Acoustic Delay Characteristic Boundary Condition (ADCBC) method. A new Averaged Proportional and Integral Linear Relaxation (APILR) method is also introduced, which modifies the Classic Linear Relaxation (CLR) method to maintain time-averaged values of inflow velocity and outflow pressure. Many moving averages may be used consecutively to increase the damping rate of boundary reflection coefficients. An integral control term is used to remove non-zero equilibrium time-averaged inflow velocities which adversely affect control over flame position in the DNS region. Both new boundary methods demonstrate their capability in inert and counterflow flames test cases. In the case of a 100 cm long tube, these methods enable the numerical simulation of combustion instabilities at 98% reduced computational expense.

title: Graph neural networks and the energetic cavity method for combinatorial optimization
summary: We study the use of graph neural networks (GNNs) for finding approximate ground states of Ising models. Efficiently finding these ground states is of broad significance because many combinatorial optimization problems can be formulated as an Ising model with the appropriate choice of couplings and fields. Exactly solving these problems is hard but there are many good heuristic methods. A lineage of these heuristics build from mean-field approximations: one approach uses the leading eigenvector of an appropriately defined matrix, another is the min-sum algorithm, also known as the energetic cavity method. Without modification, GNNs perform worse than both of these methods. We consider small modifications to the GNN to incorporate these heuristics and find that this considerably improves performance. While the modified approach is much stronger than other deep learning approaches, we still find that simulated annealing is generally as good for the same computational cost.

title: Reduction Modulo Binary Polynomials with Logarithmic Feedback Depth
comments: 20 pages. Source code and original experimental data added as ancillary files; availability statement updated. Scientific results unchanged
summary: Polynomial modular reduction is central to binary finite-field arithmetic and repeated Frobenius powering. Top-down shift/XOR folding can use few operations when the nonleading support is sparse, but a tap near the leading term creates a long feedback chain. We formulate this recurrence as inversion of a nilpotent shift operator and factor its inverse by characteristic-two Frobenius powers. The resulting Frobenius-factorized reduction (FFR) applies to every monic binary modulus without materializing a reciprocal or dense reduction matrix, and its shifts can be generated online without a persistent modulus-specific schedule. For degree $m$ and nonempty nonleading support of size $s$, with nearest-tap distance $Δ_{\min}$, FFR uses exactly $\lceil\log_2(m/Δ_{\min})\rceil$ sequential feedback stages and has scheduled work $O(ms(1+\log(m/s)))$. A portable-C evaluation on 1,096 supports through degree $131072$ identifies distinct FFR, López--Dahab, and gf2x-backed Barrett regions. On four certified irreducible moduli, FFR makes complete Rabin irreducibility testing $1.35$--$8.04$ times faster than NTL and $1.60$--$6.81$ times faster than the matched Barrett implementation.
comment: 20 pages. Source code and original experimental data added as ancillary files; availability statement updated. Scientific results unchanged

title: Generative sequence modeling for infinite memory processes via predictive states
summary: We consider estimating the one-step-ahead conditional distribution of a multivariate stochastic process. Many existing approaches rely on structural assumptions such as finite-range memory, sparsity, or additivity, which can be poorly suited to processes with long-range nonlinear interactions. However, without such structural assumptions, nonparametric estimation is known to be challenging due to the curse of dimensionality. To address this challenge, we introduce a new estimator based on the idea of learning representations of the \emph{predictive states} of a stochastic process. We theoretically analyze several aspects of this problem. As a bonus, we establish convergence rate guarantees for an instantiation of our method based on deep neural network estimators. Our results suggest that faster convergence rates are achievable when the predictive state space is lower-dimensional. That is, when the past history can be compressed into a lower-dimensional statistic that is sufficient for predicting the future. We implement our method in PyTorch and evaluate its performance on synthetic data and real \emph{C. elegans} data.

title: A depolarizing choir sings in Gaussian harmony
summary: We study the noise threshold for positive quantum capacity for the qubit depolarizing channel. We explore analytically the action of the qubit depolarizing channel on the symmetric subspaces of the input qubits, in the limit of asymptotically many uses of the channel. We observe the emergence of a bosonic Gaussian channel. Furthermore, the codes previously developed for the depolarizing channel can be translated to codes for the emergent Gaussian channel, and it is easier to further optimize these codes for the simpler emergent Gaussian channel. Translating these codes back to the depolarizing channel leads to extremely good input states for the coherent information of the depolarizing channel producing new lower bounds on the noise threshold for positive capacity. In addition to improved lower bounds on the threshold, this newly found link between depolarizing noise and Gaussian channels offers a novel perspective contributing to our understanding of these symmetric codes.

title: Non-isomorphic graphs have distinct vertex-Ramsey classes
comments: Added a result on vertex-Ramsey equivalent families of graphs. 5 pages, 1 figure
summary: For a graph $H$, its $k$-colour vertex Ramsey class is the set of all graphs $G$ such that any colouring of the vertices of $G$ in $k$ colours results in a monochromatic (induced) copy of $H$. We prove that for any $k$, the $k$-colour vertex Ramsey classes of any non-isomorphic graphs are distinct. Moreover, we show that this property does not hold when individual graphs are replaced with families of graphs.
comment: Added a result on vertex-Ramsey equivalent families of graphs. 5 pages, 1 figure

title: AEGIS: Differentiable Mars Climate Model with Neural Closures
summary: General circulation models (GCMs) are the primary tool for simulating planetary atmospheres. They play a vital role in understanding Mars's atmosphere, as forecasting its unique weather is mission-critical for operations such as entry, descent, and landing. Mars poses unusual challenges for these models, as observations are sparse compared to Earth. In addition, a thin $CO_2$ atmosphere alongside a radiatively active dust cycle creates a volatile atmosphere with large diurnal temperature swings and no true terrestrial analog for validation. Existing Mars GCMs, including the LMD PCM, the NASA Ames Mars GCM, and PlanetWRF, are mature and physically detailed but are implemented in legacy Fortran with finite-difference or finite-volume solvers, and they do not expose gradients for calibration or machine learning. Here we present AEGIS, a modular differentiable Mars climate model that couples Mars's unique atmospheric physics to the Dinosaur dynamical core, with interfaces for neural closures. We showcase stable ten-Mars-year simulations that reproduce the seasonal $CO_2$ cycle while conserving the total $CO_2$ inventory, capture realistic large-scale surface-temperature structure, and produce surface pressure that follows Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) topography. Gradients through coupled trajectories agree with finite differences and support physical calibration and neural training. We compare with conventional GCMs, highlighting the framework's computational efficiency and differentiability.

title: ECGGuard: Deep Watermarking of Electrocardiogram Signals With Error-Correcting Codes
summary: Wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings pass through multiple networks and systems before automated interpretation, leaving patient metadata vulnerable to loss. Digital watermarking can embed this metadata in the signal, but conventional methods fail under time shifts, and high waveform similarity does not guarantee the same downstream diagnosis. We present \rev{ECGGuard}, a deep watermarking framework for single-lead ECG. A fully convolutional generator embeds the payload without signal quantization, a detector decodes the message frame by frame and checks for watermark presence, and during training a frozen arrhythmia classifier penalizes changes that would alter its predictions. Because high bit accuracy does not ensure whole-message recovery, the payload is protected by extended Hamming codes, \rev{a validation-selected channel ordering}, and soft-decision decoding. On the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, \rev{averaged over three training runs, ECGGuard} keeps bit accuracy above \rev{98\%} under time shifts of 10 to 50 samples, where transform-domain baselines drop to chance. The coded 16-bit payload is recovered exactly in \rev{99.95\%} of clean segments\rev{, in over 96\%} under time shifts, 10\% sample deletion, or 10\% packet loss\rev{, and in 99.1\% for unseen subjects}. \rev{For the guiding classifier, the diagnostic loss limits the drop in ventricular-beat sensitivity to 1.6 percentage points on the test records (35.0 without it) and to 12.2 points for unseen subjects (67.0 without it); the drop grows to 10.3 points for independently trained classifiers, and the protection does not transfer to an external database.} \rev{ECGGuard} has 0.56 million parameters and needs about \rev{19}~ms per segment on a desktop CPU.

title: Not All Mislabels Are Equal: Efficient Task-Aware Auditing with Confidence Sequences
summary: We study efficient, adaptive auditing of categorical labels in a fixed dataset, motivated by biodiversity credit programs in which expert verification of species records is costly and downstream scores (e.g., payment) are more sensitive to errors on certain labels than on others. Our proposed ATLAS framework couples anytime-valid inference with a task-aware adaptive auditing policy. Representing label corrections through a confusion matrix, we prioritize which data points to inspect next based on both label uncertainty and the influence of potential label corrections on the downstream score function. In our main case study on Kenyan biodiversity data, task-aware auditing reduces the expert review needed to estimate both the mislabel rate and the nonlinear biodiversity score while maintaining anytime-valid guarantees. We also evaluate ATLAS on public datasets for image classification and named-entity recognition. Across our experiments with linear and nonlinear scores, ATLAS generally reaches the same precision as competing anytime-valid methods with substantially fewer audits. When distribution-free guarantees are prohibitively costly, we develop a model-based Bayesian alternative that can further reduce the number of audits by relying on modeling assumptions. Our biodiversity case study highlights a gap between statistical validity and practical feasibility: generic methods such as Serfling's bound and existing confidence-sequence procedures are rigorous but can require prohibitively many expert reviews in practice. Together, these results show task-aware auditing can significantly reduce the number of expert audits needed while providing finite-sample, anytime-valid guarantees

title: Formalizing the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes by a Generalized Notion of Co-dimension
summary: In this work, we formalize the concept of intrinsic dimension of objective landscapes introduced in Li et al. (2018), which measures the structural complexity of learning problems by training along randomly generated subspaces. We define the intrinsic dimension of a set $Θ\subset\mathbb{R}^p$ as the minimal dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(Θ)$ such that a random plane of dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(Θ)$ in $\mathbb{R}^p$ intersects $Θ$ with probability one. We show that it is a generalized notion of co-dimension that depends on the global geometry of $Θ$. We study mathematical properties of the intrinsic dimension and develop techniques to estimate the intrinsic dimension of sets $Θ$ that arise in learning problems. More specifically, we derive upper and/or lower bounds where $Θ$ is the set of optimal parameters in student-teacher settings with shallow and deep ReLU networks, including finite and infinite sample cases, and with and without regularization. We discuss how our theory leads to novel types of generalization bounds, thereby showing that the intrinsic dimension is a measure of learning complexity. Our results connect techniques from seemingly different areas of machine learning research such as classification of symmetries of ReLU networks and stochastic geometry.

title: Optimal self-orthogonal binary linear codes
comments: 40 pages; typos corrected; comments more than welcome
summary: We complete the determination of the minimum possible length of eight-dimensional binary self-orthogonal codes with given minimum distance. For dimension nine we give exact values and bounds for minimum distance at most $64$. By exploiting the geometric reformulation of linear codes as multisets of points, we fully redo the classification for dimension at most seven in a simplified and computer-free manner. As a by-product we prove the non-existence of $[93,9,44]_2$ codes and show several divisibility results for putative optimal nine-dimensional binary codes.
comment: 40 pages; typos corrected; comments more than welcome

title: Sampling Design and Confidence Tubes for Integral Curves on Riemannian Manifolds
summary: We estimate the integral curve of an unknown vector field from noisy tangent vector field on a known compact Riemannian manifold. We consider two sampling settings: independent observations at random locations that have already been collected, and a fixed response budget that allows subsequent locations to be chosen using pilot information. Under suitable regularity assumptions, the passive kernel estimator has curve error of order $n^{-2/(d+3)}$ in probability, with sample size $n$ and manifold dimension $d$. Its functional central limit theorem has a limit characterized by a linear stochastic differential equation. For active sampling, an independent pilot directs one new batch of measurements to neighborhoods of the target curve. Under localization, smoothness and design conditions, this concentration yields expected maximum curve error of order $N^{-1/2}$, including the pilot in the total response budget $N$. Both methods provide simultaneous geodesic confidence tubes with asymptotically exact coverage under mild conditions. Simulations show narrower active tubes in most reported settings, with improved small-sample coverage in some three-dimensional examples. Ocean-drifter observations illustrate mean-flow reconstruction on the sphere, and a canopy-flow LDA application uses retrospective active sampling to quantify lateral and vertical departures of local mean streamlines.

title: Rotating Walks, Derandomized Squares, and Permutation Conjugated Walks
summary:
Using the recent strong convergence results of Bordenave and Collins (Annals of Mathematics) and Chen et al. (Annals of Mathematics), we study the average case behavior of rotating random walks of Cohen and Maor (STOC 2023) and the derandomized square construction of Rozenman and Vadhan (RANDOM 2005).
  Concretely, we prove a conjecture of Cohen et al. (ITCS 2025) regarding the average case behavior of derandomized squaring for random graphs and show that the existential bounds of Cohen and Maor for their rotating random walk construction hold with high-probability for random graphs. Using the results of O'Donnell and Wu (FOCS 2020), we can in polynomial time construct a family of graphs and rotations which almost saturate the bounds of Cohen and Maor, and meet the bounds conjectured by Cohen et al. for all vertex-transitive auxiliary graphs of fixed degree in the derandomized square.
  Finally, we study independent random permutation conjugates of deterministic regular graph adjacency matrices. We prove quantitative weak convergence to freely independent tree adjacency operators when the degrees are fixed and the girths tend to infinity. Separately, a covering argument gives deterministic spectral lower bounds for polynomials with non-negative coefficients, recovering the lower bound of Cohen et al. for rotating walks.

title: Asymptotic Dimension of Persistence Modules of Bounded Presentation
comments: 22 pages. Companion paper: arXiv:2611.12866. v2: new Section 9 proves the position count under the matching distance; revised introduction and discussion
summary: We compute the asymptotic dimension of spaces of multiparameter persistence modules of bounded presentation under the interleaving distance. The $d$-parameter modules with at most $n$ generators and $m$ relations have asymptotic dimension, and Assouad-Nagata dimension, exactly $d(n+m)$, the number of coordinates of their generator and relation grades, over every field; for two parameters this is $2(n+m)$. The space has continuous moduli, already for two parameters and $n,m\ge2$: over an infinite field it contains, at every scale, infinite uniformly separated families of pairwise non-isomorphic modules with one fibered barcode, so it is not doubling even at a fixed fibered barcode; already for $m\ge1$ it is not coarsely equivalent to a proper metric space. The proof is an induction on the number of distinct grade coordinates: an interleaving small compared with the gaps between these coordinates moves each of them by at most twice its size and preserves the induced grid representation, so the continuous moduli are invisible at large scale. Each class of modules at finite distance therefore embeds coarsely into Hilbert space; for two parameters, $n,m\ge2$ and an uncountable field, a class containing such a family admits no coarse embedding into a separable Hilbert space. Under the two-parameter matching distance, on the space of rank invariants, the asymptotic dimension and the Assouad-Nagata dimension are again $2(n+m)$: slope-one slices pin the grid of grades, and over a grid only finitely many rank invariants occur; on a finite net of $S$ slices the asymptotic dimension is at most $2nS$.
comment: 22 pages. Companion paper: arXiv:2611.12866. v2: new Section 9 proves the position count under the matching distance; revised introduction and discussion

title: Device-Centric Cooperative Floor-Level Estimation under Sparse Anchor Deployment for Construction-Site Applications
summary: For construction-site applications in multi-story buildings, accurate floor-level estimation is important for tracking workers, equipment, and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. In buildings under construction, communication infrastructure and power-supply facilities are often limited and the indoor environment changes as construction progresses, making localization systems that rely on dense wireless infrastructure or fingerprint databases difficult to deploy and maintain. Low-power wide-area (LPWA) communication can provide wide-area coverage with a small number of temporarily deployed access points (APs), but under sparse AP deployment, AP-to-terminal observations alone may provide insufficient floor-related information for reliable floor-level estimation. To address this problem, this paper develops a device-centric cooperative floor-level estimation method that exploits inter-terminal observations as relative floor-difference information to complement AP-side information. For practical application with limited measurement data, AP-to-terminal observations are represented by an upper/lower-AP RSS contrast, while inter-terminal observations are statistically modeled according to floor-difference classes. The resulting AP-side and pairwise scores are combined in a weighted floor-label objective and approximately optimized using dual-order sequential iterated conditional modes (ICM). Ray-tracing simulations and LoRa measurement experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method under different AP deployments and terminal-selection limits.

title: Virtual EMI Receiver Generation (VERGE) for Improved EMI Removal in MRI
summary: MRI is not designed to operate in the presence of EMI emitting electronic devices. To accomodate this, we propose VERGE which improves on previous EMI removal methods and can operate without external EMI sensors. VERGE estimates a reference coil non-linearly from all imaging and non-imaging coils by training a small per-scan convolutional neural net to generate a virtual coil. The virtual coil is then used with STRIDE, a reference-based EMI removal method. For single-source EMI contamination, VERGE performed similarly to the reference method. For multi-source dynamic EMI contamination, VERGE outperformed the comparison methods. Notably, VERGE with zero physical EMI sensors outperformed the comparison methods even with two physical EMI sensors. A non-linearly estimated virtual EMI coil improves reference-coil-based EMI removal under dynamic multi-source EMI, and enables effective EMI removal without physical EMI sensors or training data.

title: Hardware Impairment Parameter Estimation in Fluid Antenna Systems by Inverse Optimization
summary: In this paper, the problem of estimating the hardware impairment parameters of fluid antennas (FAs) in a multi-base station (BS) multi-user communication system is studied. The actual hardware coefficients are unknown, whereas the FA positions and transmit beamforming vectors adopted by the BSs are known. We first formulate a forward spectral efficiency (SE) maximization problem and introduce aggregate interference variables whose consistency with the physical inter-cell interference can be maintained through a pricing mechanism. For inverse estimation, the aggregate interference is obtained from receiver-side interference measurements associated with the observed network decisions. We then construct a trust-region linear model of the position-update problem around the observed FA positions. To extend the applicability of the proposed framework to antenna positions obtained from inexact or heuristic algorithms, we develop an inverse optimization model with an explicit duality-gap tolerance, which is solved using sequential quadratic programming (SQP). Simulation results show that the proposed scheme attains a lower estimation error than KKT residual minimization (KKT-RM) at both considered transmit-power levels and improves the SE by up to 22.86% over the Ideal-hardware-assumption scheme.

title: Edge-Combining Subharmonic Mixer-First Receiver
summary: A 1-10 GHz subharmonic mixer-first receiver using edge combining to drive N-path switches from 50% duty-cycle clocks at half the local oscillator (LO) frequency avoids the gain penalty of harmonic mixing. Inverter-based differential baseband amplifiers with back-gate feedback linearization set their gain by process-defined capacitance ratios, using no additional components and consuming no additional power. A 22 nm fully depleted silicon on insulator (FD-SOI) prototype receiver achieves a conversion gain of 12.8-18.1 dB and a noise figure of 5.7-11 dB across the band. It achieves up to 15.4 dBm out-of-band IIP3 while consuming 16.7-22.3 mW.

title: Least ln-cosh-based adaptive filtering algorithm for graph signal processing
comments: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems
summary: Currently, an increasing number of irregular signals are being defined within graph structures. This paper proposes a Least ln-cosh-based Adaptive Filtering for Graph Signal Processing (GSP LLAF) algorithm for offline/online graph signal estimation under various non-Gaussian noise conditions. Compared to the recently proposed Graph Adaptive Least Mean p-th Power (GSP LMP) algorithm, GSP LLAF eliminates the need for prior knowledge of the noise characteristics. Simultaneously, GSP LLAF addresses the limitation in estimation accuracy encountered by the Sign Algorithm for Graph Signal Processing (GSP Sign) and the Graph Signal Processing algorithm based on the Generalized Maximum Correntropy Criterion (GSP GMCC). Furthermore, the algorithm features low computational complexity and fast execution speed. To achieve a balance between convergence speed and estimation accuracy, a variable step-size variant, the Modified Variable Step-Size Least ln-cosh-based Adaptive Filtering Algorithm for Graph Signal Processing (GSP MVSS-LLAF), is proposed. In estimation experiments involving both static and time-varying graph signals, the proposed GSP LLAF and GSP MVSS-LLAF algorithms demonstrate fast, stable, and robust graph signal estimation performance under various non-Gaussian noise conditions, including Bernoulli-Gaussian (BG) modeled impulse noise, as well as alpha-stable, Cauchy, and Laplace distributions.
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems

title: Robust DOA Estimation for GNSS-like Signals Under Jamming: A Rotation-Enhanced SWN-MUSIC Approach
summary: In jamming environments, accurate direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation for Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-like signals using antenna arrays is crucial for spoofing detection and subsequent countermeasures. However, estimation accuracy strongly depends on the incident direction of the signal of interest (SOI) under a given jamming and array configuration, with severe errors occurring in certain directions---a phenomenon whose physical mechanisms remain unclear. To address this gap, we identify two types of geometric ill-conditions between the array manifold and the jamming subspace, clarifying that certain directions suffer from inherently unfavorable observation geometry, which cannot be overcome by algorithmic refinement alone. Motivated by this insight, we introduce a paradigm namely rotational diversity, which treats the array attitude as a controllable sensing resource to actively reconfigure the observation geometry, thereby providing complementary perspectives in which the problematic directions can be accurately estimated. To implement this paradigm, we develop a Rotation-Enhanced Spatial Whitening and Normalized Multiple Signal Classification (SWN-MUSIC) framework, which performs independent DOA estimations across multiple rotation angles and selectively integrates reliable estimates. Simulation results demonstrate substantial improvement in accuracy in the directions that were poorly estimated under the fixed-array SWN-MUSIC, while maintaining performance in well-conditioned directions, thereby producing more robust DOA estimates.

title: Personalized Causal Low-Bitrate Coded Speech Restoration with Speaker Embeddings
summary: Legacy low-bitrate speech codecs such as AMR-NB remain widely used in telephony, where they restrict speech bandwidth and degrade listening quality. Coded speech restoration (CSR) aims to restore the speech bandwidth while improving the overall quality of coded speech, but typically without adapting to different speakers. In this paper, we systematically investigate personalization for restoration of speech coded at low bitrates, using a causal, low-complexity Universal Bandwidth Extension Generative Adversarial Network (UBGAN) model as the basis. We propose two personalization methods based on speaker embeddings, which incur little additional computational cost at inference: (i) conditioning a single CSR model on speaker embeddings, and (ii) cluster-based model selection, where multiple personalized models are trained on clusters of acoustically similar speakers. Experiments are performed on AMR-NB coded speech at 4.75 kbps. Experimental results with disjoint seen- and unseen-speaker test sets show that cluster-based model selection does not consistently outperform the non-personalized UBGAN baseline, whereas embedding conditioning significantly improves ViSQOL and WB-PESQ scores for both seen and unseen speakers.

title: Reference Coordinates, Output Perturbations, and Information Loss in EEG Decoding
comments: 45 pages including supplementary material; 5 figures in the main text. Data and code included as ancillary material
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) decoders can respond to reference changes that preserve all relative-potential information. We use established measurement-operator theory to distinguish coordinate sensitivity, additional output-channel perturbations, and electrode loss. Exact pseudoinverse alignment supplies a consistency control; measurement-operator canonicalization (MOC) denotes a graph-Tikhonov estimator. The broader evaluation covers three public motor-imagery datasets and four decoders. The primary EEGNet comparison on Cho2017 and PhysioNet uses three paired training seeds, three shared noise realizations, and six front ends, with identical CAR training inputs sharing checkpoints. At 10 dB output perturbation, MOC-minus-raw disagreement was -0.144 and -0.107, while balanced-accuracy differences were 0.044 and 0.050, respectively; these four contrasts passed the retained Holm correction. MOC also reduced disagreement relative to pseudoinversion across all three seeds in both cohorts. However, comparison with fixed graph smoothing after pseudoinversion did not establish an additional MOC benefit. Preserving zero reference rows changed raw disagreement by less than 0.001 in magnitude; inverse-method predictions were unchanged. For canonical front ends, cross-reference disagreement was close to the reference obtained from independent noise within the same operator. Controlled weak-mode reconstruction and equal-rank electrode masks exposed separate stability and information-loss effects. The results locate the complete-reference gains within spatial processing under the specified stress model, while requiring decoding accuracy alongside consistency to assess practical utility.
comment: 45 pages including supplementary material; 5 figures in the main text. Data and code included as ancillary material

title: Structured Design of Layered Sparse Unitary Space-Time Modulation for Integrated Noncoherent and Coherent MIMO Communications
summary: This work presents a novel structured constellation design based on unitary space-time modulation (USTM) for integrated noncoherent and coherent multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communications. Information is encoded into the sparse space-time matrices through two layers: a noncoherent layer that distinguishes points on the Grassmann manifold (subspaces) and a coherent layer that distinguishes among the Stiefel representatives associated with each of those points (bases for the subspaces). We consider sequential decoding of the two layers to reduce computational complexity, while explicitly identifying the matrix structures that favor this decoding strategy. The proposed constellation builds on a previous structured Grassmannian signaling design, which has the remarkable property of producing space-time matrices with a single nonzero entry per row, while introducing a novel systematic design for the second layer corresponding to the Stiefel representatives. The design of the second layer preserves the sparsity of the first layer and significantly reduces the decoding computational complexity, while ensuring reliable performance under sequential decoding and enabling a simple yet effective bit labeling, as validated by numerical results in terms of bit error rate (BER) and symbol error rate (SER). Numerical results also show graceful performance degradation under channel correlation and, for limited coherence intervals where channel state information at the receiver (CSIR) can be estimated only imperfectly, improved performance compared with classical space-time block coding (STBC) schemes based on QAM and PSK.

title: Generation of Sample Complex Wishart Distributed Matrices and Change Detection in Polarimetric SAR Data
summary: The complex Wishart distribution is used to describe synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data in the so-called covariance matrix representation. We give a test statistic for detection of differences between two instances in this distribution and an associated probability measure. Generated complex Wishart distributed covariance matrices are used to show that this test statistic and the probability measure in situations with no differences follow the expected distributions.

title: Distributed Blind Source Separation from Compressed Mixtures
summary: Blind source separation (BSS) is increasingly needed in sensing architectures where mixtures are acquired by multiple remote devices but the inference itself is carried out centrally. In such systems, the sensors often cannot transmit their raw observations since the communication links are rate-limited, energy-limited, or both. The fusion center therefore must recover the latent sources from compressed versions of the mixtures. This setting raises questions that classical BSS models do not address directly: whether source identifiability survives compression, how separation accuracy changes under a specified compression model, and how the separation procedure should be modified to account for the statistical model induced by the compression stage. In this work, we develop a framework for distributed BSS from compressed mixtures that addresses these issues at three levels. First, we formalize identifiability under compression and establish a data-processing viewpoint showing that compression cannot introduce distinguishability that is absent before compression. Second, for mixtures of Gaussian sources with general covariance structures, we derive an idealized Gaussian rate-distortion-based Cramér-Rao lower bound benchmark for the interference-to-source ratio. Third, we develop practical compression-aware separation schemes based on subtractively dithered quantization together with debiasing at the fusion center for both fourth-order-cumulant-based and second-order-statistics-based methods. Simulation experiments demonstrate the resulting tradeoffs between communication rate and separation performance and the gains obtained by compression-aware separation in representative distributed sensing scenarios.

title: Joint BS Deployment and Power Optimization for Minimum EMF Exposure with RL in Real-World Based Urban Scenario
summary: Base station (BS) deployment remains a critical task with successive wireless communication generations and increasing data rates demands, while the electromagnetic field (EMF) exposure is often underrated. Therefore, this paper proposes a workflow that adjusts BS deployment and radiated power in a 3D urban scenario to jointly consider EMF exposure and coverage. To achieve this ambition, firstly, a novel least-time shoot-and-bounce ray (SBR) ray-launching (RL) tool is developed to improve computational efficiency, and simultaneously enhance diffraction modeling for accurate EMF exposure calculation, validated with real-world measurements. To efficiently extend the computation across the target urban area, the adaptive grid refinement (AGR) algorithm is designed based on the spatial stability of the effective channel while accounting for BS beamforming. Subsequently, to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of EMF exposure under practical network operations, a system-level abstraction further accounts for the actual maximum transmit power, intercell interference, and channel state information imperfection on the BS side, while capturing mobility over the EMF exposure averaging interval on the user equipment side. Upon the aforementioned aspects, the coverage-guaranteed EMF exposure minimization problem is formulated in a realistic and accurate manner, and solved by a geometry-aware algorithm that enables joint BS deployment and power optimization based on deterministic channel simulations under practical deployment constraints, completing the proposed workflow. Simulation results illustrate the application of the workflow in the considered urban scenario, while comparison with an empirical baseline highlights that the workflow mitigates EMF exposure underestimation and yields BS deployment configurations better aligned with real-world conditions.

title: From High-Level Communication Requirements to KPIs via Conformal Signal Temporal Logic Learning
summary: Softwarized radio access networks (RANs), such as those based on the Open RAN (O-RAN) architecture, generate rich streams of key performance indicators (KPIs) that can be leveraged to extract actionable intelligence for network optimization. However, bridging the gap between low-level KPI measurements and high-level requirements, such as quality of experience (QoE), requires methods that are both relevant, capturing temporal patterns predictive of user-level outcomes, and interpretable, providing human-readable insights that operators can validate and act upon. This paper introduces conformal signal temporal logic learning (C-STLL), a framework that addresses both requirements. C-STLL leverages signal temporal logic (STL), a formal language for specifying temporal properties of time series, to learn from data interpretable formulas that characterize key properties of KPI traces satisfying high-level requirements. We first formulate the problem of reliably identifying an accurate STL formula as a risk-averse inference problem. We show that the optimal solution requires the construction of a set of STL formulas with formal coverage guarantees. Based on this theoretical insight, the proposed C-STLL extracts from calibration data a set of STL formulas with such guarantees via Learn Then Test, while also filtering for formula complexity and diversity. Experiments on a mobile gaming scenario in ns-3 and on KPI traces measured on a softwarized RAN testbed demonstrate that C-STLL effectively controls risk below target levels, while returning interpretable temporal specifications that relate KPI behavior to QoE outcomes.

title: Movable Antenna for Anti-Jamming Transmission: Continuous and Discrete Positioning Designs
summary: Movable antenna (MA) system holds big promise in further wireless communications due to the ability of reconfiguring the antenna position to enhance the spatial diversity. This paper investigates the joint design of beamforming and antenna positions in MA-assisted anti-jamming communications. We consider a multi-user multiple-input multiple-output downlink scenario where multiple malicious jammers exist. The goal is to maximize the sum-rate under the imperfect jammer channel state information. Then, we develop two distinct optimization frameworks for continuous and discrete antenna position designs, respectively. For the continuous position design, we propose an alternating optimization (AO) framework that integrates successive convex approximation and majorization minimization (MM) to handle the highly non-convex problem. For the discrete position design, based on the minimum mean squared error criterion and MM, we reformulate the problem as a sparse recovery task and propose a low-complexity heuristic block coordinate descent and simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit, which enables joint design rather than AO. Numerical results show that the proposed discrete-position heuristic achieves higher sum rates than the adopted AO-based continuous-position algorithm. This observation highlights the trade-off between spatial resolution and optimization tractability, indicating that the sparse-recovery formulation can yield better performance than the continuous AO algorithm in the MA-assisted anti-jamming scenarios.

title: Joint Synchronization and Radar Parameter Estimation for OFDM-based DISAC Systems
summary: We propose a novel approach to the synchronization paradigm in distributed ISAC (DISAC) systems in doubly-dispersive (DD) channel environments via a joint synchronization and radar parameter estimation framework. The proposed method exploits the structure of the system model, which can be linearized in order to apply a bivariate Gaussian belief propagation (GaBP) algorithm that jointly estimates the time offset (TO) and carrier frequency offset (CFO) of each base station (BS), as well as the delay and Doppler parameters of the DD channel in conventional orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, showing that the radar parameter estimates (i.e., range and velocity) and synchronization parameter estimates (i.e., TO and CFO) approach the Cramér Rao lower bound (CRLB) even at moderate-to-high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regimes.

title: Open-H-RF: A Large-Scale Ultrasound Raw Channel Dataset Initiative
comments: Preprint: 15 pages, 15 figures, 3 tables. Dataset (v1.1): https://open-h.github.io/Open-H-RF
summary: Medical ultrasound is a widely accessible, real-time imaging modality, yet progress in data-driven ultrasound research is constrained by the scarcity of large, open collections of raw channel data. Existing public datasets are predominantly based on reconstructed images, while the smaller number of open raw channel datasets is generally specialized to individual reconstruction or imaging tasks, limiting the development of general-purpose methods and foundation models that operate directly on ultrasound signals. While interpretive tasks can be performed on reconstructed images, many of the key technical challenges in ultrasound imaging, such as aberration correction and reverberation reduction, require the raw channel data itself. We introduce Open-H-RF, a community-driven open dataset initiative comprising approximately 40 TB of medical ultrasound raw channel data in 19,332 acquisitions, contributed by 39 institutions across academia and industry, spanning in-vivo, phantom, and simulated data. Each dataset is annotated with a number of supported tasks, ranging from generalized reconstruction, speed-of-sound estimation, and aberration correction to blood flow imaging, motion estimation, quantitative ultrasound, and image interpretation. Open-H-RF provides a unified, self-contained data format that captures raw channel data together with the acquisition, probe, metadata, and reconstruction information required for reproducible processing across scanners and acquisition schemes. The corpus is publicly hosted under a permissive CC BY 4.0 license and can be streamed programmatically and selectively at scale. By bringing heterogeneous ultrasound data into a common representation, backed by modern data infrastructure, Open-H-RF lowers the barrier to working with raw channel data and aims to open medical ultrasound research to new communities. See https://open-h.github.io/Open-H-RF.

title: Decoding Motion-Blurred QR Codes: Motion-Parameter Error Tolerance and Model-Based Recovery
summary: In automated manufacturing, logistics, and inspection, Quick Response (QR) codes are often read on the fly under continuous ambient light without active strobes or motion pauses. The resulting relative three-dimensional motion produces spatially varying blur that defeats standard decoders, yet how accurately the motion must be estimated to recover the payload remains an open question. To address this question from a task-driven evaluation perspective centered on machine recognition effectiveness, we formulate motion-blurred QR recovery within a unified mathematical framework of identifiability. Within this framework, we systematically measure the decoding tolerance to perturbations in motion length, direction, rotation or scaling centre, and speed profile. These controlled experiments reveal three structural laws: 1) parameter tolerances shrink rapidly as blur amplitude grows and are tightest under uniform speed, whereas accelerating motion is substantially more forgiving; 2) length tolerance can differ markedly between underestimation and overestimation; 3) errors that are individually benign interact strongly and prevent decoding when combined. Guided by these findings, we propose a grey-box recovery pipeline in which two compact networks predict an initial corner trajectory, followed by tolerance-guided candidate search, alternating image-and-path fitting, and regularised linear inversion. On a benchmark of 955 real motion-blurred photographs spanning four camera models and four rigid-motion families, our method recovers the exact payload on 93.1% of the images. It outperforms the strongest fine-tuned deblurring network at 83.6% and reduces the decoding error rate by 58.0%, with zero wrong strings accepted.

title: When to Move: Online Repositioning of Movable Antenna Arrays Under a Long-Term Actuation Energy Budget
comments: This work was intended as a replacement of arXiv:2609.25439 and any subsequent updates will appear there
summary: Movable antenna (MA) arrays improve multiuser throughput by repositioning their elements, but mechanical movement reduces transmission time and consumes actuation energy. Changes in user configurations create nonuniform demand for repositioning over time, while each movement determines which positions are reachable in subsequent slots. Thus, online control must decide when to spend a limited actuation-energy budget, not only where to position the antennas. We formulate causal effective-throughput maximization under displacement-dependent movement delay, inter-slot reachability, and a long-term average actuation-energy constraint. We propose Lyapunov-based online movable-antenna repositioning (LOMA), which adjusts the price of movement through a virtual queue and solves the resulting nonconvex position problem via proximal minorization--maximization, accounting for nonsmooth movement delay and promoting sparse antenna updates. We establish monotone ascent of the smoothed per-slot objective, a finite-horizon sample-path energy bound, almost-sure long-term budget feasibility under a Gaussian fading model with bounded large-scale gains, and a state-matched throughput comparison separating temporal energy allocation from per-slot optimization error. Simulations show that LOMA concentrates actuation after intermittent user changes and improves effective throughput over optimized fixed arrays and a per-slot-budget counterpart, while continuous channel drift favors more frequent incremental repositioning. Additional simulations with pilot-based channel estimates in sparse millimeter-wave channels show that LOMA retains most of the throughput benefits of online repositioning while operating near its prescribed long-term actuation-energy budget.

title: Wideband overlapped polyphase channelizer for kinetic inductance detector readout: split-path architecture and experimental characterization
comments: 18 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to Measurement (Elsevier). v2: revised and retitled version that adds the experimental characterization on the board (v1, submitted to JATIS, was titled "A high-isolation wideband channelizer for MKID readouts: a custom HLS implementation on RFSoC"). Extends Proc. SPIE 14156, 141561I (doi:10.1117/12.3103240)
summary: Frequency-multiplexed readout of kinetic inductance detector arrays measures the complex transmission of thousands of superconducting resonators. The channelizer that separates them introduces systematic effects: a gain that depends on where each tone falls in the channel grid, leakage between channels and added noise. This article presents a 4096-channel polyphase channelizer with 2/1 overlap for a 4.096 GS/s input, implemented on a first-generation radio-frequency system-on-chip, and a procedure to characterize it on the board with two receive chains, one digitizing the excitation as a reference. A split-path architecture computes the two overlap states in parallel filter branches at 256 MHz and reorders them frame by frame, under three control rules; it keeps only the transform stage at 512 MHz and affords a prototype of 16 taps per polyphase path (65536 coefficients) at the multiplication rate of a published 8-tap bank. Each selected channel is exported as a complex series at 1 MS/s. The measured channel response follows the coefficient-table model within 0.15 dB down to -28 dB, with both overlapping channels at full gain across their common band. Leakage into every measured channel 1.875 MHz or more from the tone is -94 dBc or lower, apart from images attributed to converter interleaving. The signal-to-noise ratio per sample lies within 1.7 dB of the limit set by the data-sheet noise density of the converter, and an emulated detector pulse is recovered with a decay time of 14.65 $μ$s (standard uncertainty 0.04 $μ$s), within 0.7% of the expected value.

title: Deep Learning Models for Fractional Option Pricing
summary: This paper investigates whether neural networks can infer fractional option prices and the Hurst parameter directly from sequences of fractional Gaussian returns, without separately estimating the latent parameters for each new sequence. Feedforward neural networks (FNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are trained to jointly predict European call prices, put prices, and the Hurst parameter from 252-return sequences. A controlled simulation varies the total sample size from 5,000 to 500,000 sequences and evaluates point prediction, empirical residual-based prediction intervals, and computational performance. The neural-network models are also compared on a common simulated test set with Bayesian joint estimation and exact Gaussian maximum likelihood estimation. In that four-method comparison, the LSTM achieves the lowest Hurst-parameter root mean squared error (0.033) and option-price root mean squared error (1.305). After training, neural-network predictions are substantially faster than repeated parameter estimation, although the methods quantify uncertainty in different ways. Applications to five financial return series illustrate differences between data-driven and model-based fractional price estimates. The results support sequence-based learning as a computationally efficient complement to statistical inference under the assumed fractional model; they do not establish out-of-distribution accuracy or accuracy against observed traded-option prices.

title: Copula-Based Synthetic Data Generation: A Use-Inspired Perspective on Trade-offs
summary: The generation of synthetic data offers a promising way to address challenges related to data scarcity and privacy concerns. While many approaches have been developed, tabular synthetic data generation methods often require complex models and extensive training data, while lacking interpretability. In this work, we investigate versatile probabilistic approaches using copulas, and leverage in particular the Gaussian Mixture Copula Model, to model the joint distribution of multivariate data, with a main focus on moderate-dimensional data sets. Taking a use-inspired perspective, we examine key trade-offs inherent to synthetic data evaluation, spanning fidelity, utility, and privacy, and demonstrate that copula-based methods achieve a sound balance across all three dimensions while remaining interpretable and providing an explicit probabilistic model. We illustrate and highlight the potential benefits of the method on a test case focusing on systematic missing values in a cardiovascular risk calculator and develop specific evaluation metrics for this application.

title: JALE: A new Python toolbox for coordinate-based neuroimaging meta-analysis using activation likelihood estimation
summary: Coordinate-based neuroimaging meta-analysis using activation likelihood estimation (ALE) is commonly used to synthesize reported results of functional or structural magnetic resonance imaging studies. We here present JALE, a new, open-source Python package for conducting ALE meta-analyses. Besides computing standard ALE main effects and contrast analyses, this toolbox implements several novel analytical approaches including new options for thresholding (threshold-free cluster enhancement statistics, significance threshold prediction) as well as sensitivity and cluster analyses that were only available as in-house scripts in the past. The purpose of this paper is to provide an integrated conceptual foundation of recent developments in the ALE meta-analysis framework, with a particular focus on novel methodological implementations that can be executed in a straightforward and standardized manner using the new JALE toolbox.

title: Milk yield responses to heat stress in tropical dairy cattle
authors: Marcos Vinicius Gualberto Barbosa da Silva
summary:
Context: Rising temperatures and warm tropical nights threaten dairy productivity and resilience across tropical landscapes.
  Objective: This study characterises multi-scale interactions among thermal regimes, nighttime cooling, metabolic heat load, and crossbred genetics on daily milk yield in Brazilian dairy systems.
  Methods: A 24-year panel (2001--2024) of 788,528 test-day records from 87,809 Girolando (Holstein $\times$ Gyr) cows across 408 municipalities was linked to weather data. Two-way fixed effects, distributed lag, and piecewise threshold spline models were estimated across yield quartiles and crossbred fractions.
  Results: While aggregate summaries suggest stable yield up to a daily mean Temperature--Humidity Index (THI) of 76, production-stratified splines show high-yielding cows lose milk starting at THI 68 and accelerating above 76 ($-0.162$ kg animal$^{-1}$ d$^{-1}$ unit$^{-1}$, $p=0.0062$), whereas low-yielding cows remain unaffected ($p=0.81$). Distributed lag models reveal an immediate drop followed by a deeper trough four days later. Lack of nighttime relief ($\mathrm{THI}_{\min} \ge 68$) reduces yield by an extra 2.37 kg animal$^{-1}$ d$^{-1}$ ($p \le 0.001$) and causes an 8.6\% loss after seven warm nights, whereas wide diurnal amplitude buffers output by $+1.60$ kg animal$^{-1}$ d$^{-1}$. At comparable high yields ($\approx 31$ kg animal$^{-1}$ d$^{-1}$), intermediate crossbreds ($1/2$ and $5/8$ Holstein) sustain yield up to THI 76, whereas $7/8$ Holstein cows decline at THI 68.
  Conclusions: Tropical dairy adaptation requires continuous nighttime cooling for high-yielding cows combined with balanced Zebu--taurine crossbreeding.

title: Deep Mixture Models: A Statistical Review with R
summary: Deep mixture models extend finite mixture models through hierarchical latent factor structures with shared mixture parameters. This focused review examines deep Gaussian mixture models (DGMMs), robust deep mixture models (RDMMs), deep skew-$t$ mixture models (DStMMs), and mixed deep Gaussian mixture models (MDGMMs) within a common statistical framework. We compare their pathway distributions, measurement models, and latent architectures, highlighting the implications for likelihood evaluation and inference. For continuous measurements, we discuss Gaussian conditional calculations and the scale-mixture methods underlying Student-$t$ and skew-$t$ pathways. For mixed measurements, we consider response-specific likelihoods and numerical integration for discrete variables. Alongside the review, we introduce \texttt{MixedDeepMM}, an R package providing a unified interface for fitting and evaluating deep mixture models with Gaussian, Student-$t$, and skew-$t$ kernels, supporting continuous and mixed measurements and single- and two-head architectures. We illustrate its use on the UCI Wine and Cryotherapy datasets, reporting clustering measures with standard errors across repeated fits and visualising consensus partitions. For mixed data, Gower silhouette widths complement external clustering agreement measures. We conclude by discussing computational challenges, model selection, and uncertainty assessment.

title: TRAIL-IRL: Crossed Reward-Temperature Mixtures for Unlabeled Trajectory Clustering
summary: Different paths need not imply different preferences, trajectories also differ in how randomly actions are chosen. Many multi-reward inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) methods assume common action randomness and can confound it with preference heterogeneity. We introduce TRAIL-IRL, which clusters unlabeled trajectories using rewards for preferences and temperatures for action randomness. Its crossed mixture pairs each reward with a shared set of temperature levels, allowing action regularity to vary within preference groups. With centered and normalized rewards in a known finite-state environment, we establish the identifiability conditions under which the distribution of sufficiently long trajectories determines rewards, temperatures, mixing weights, and class counts up to relabeling. Under the same conditions and reward constraints, common-temperature reward mixtures with the same component count cannot reproduce a crossed mixture with multiple temperatures. We develop a generalized expectation-maximization algorithm and select class counts using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). Simulations show improved predictive fit, reward recovery, and trajectory classification over common-temperature mixtures with the same component count. For 140 bird-year trajectories from 79 white storks, BIC favors four reward classes and three temperature levels over common-temperature candidates. Younger birds have higher posterior membership probabilities for a southwestward migration class, whereas older birds have higher probabilities for a northern retention class. Within reward classes, higher temperatures are associated with more variable movement directions and positions farther ahead along the migration route, consistent with social information use and collective sensing.

title: A Bayesian Framework for Latent Compliance Modeling in Cluster Randomized Trials with One-Sided Noncompliance
summary: In pragmatic cluster randomized controlled trials (PCRCTs), healthcare providers are randomized, but intervention delivery and patient receipt may vary after assignment. In many PCRCTs, cluster-level implementation is measured using continuous implementation metrics, while individual compliance is recorded as a binary indicator. Standard complier average causal effect (CACE) estimands focus on individual-level compliance and do not account for heterogeneity in implementation across clusters. When intervention uptake is shaped by both cluster- and individual-level processes, it is of scientific interest to characterize how effects vary across these sources of compliance. We propose a Bayesian framework for PCRCTs with one-sided binary noncompliance at the individual level and one-sided partial compliance at the cluster level. The method uses a latent mixture model to summarize heterogeneity in cluster-level implementation based on baseline characteristics and treatment-arm implementation measures, and links these latent implementation strata to individual compliance and outcomes through a joint model. Because individual compliance and treatment-defined implementation measures are observed only under treatment assignment, the model imputes these quantities for control clusters and individuals assigned to control. The framework enables estimation of finite- and super-population intent-to-treat (ITT) and CACE estimands, both marginally and within latent implementation strata. We apply the method to the METRIcAL trial, a pragmatic cluster randomized study evaluating a personalized music intervention for nursing home residents with dementia. The analysis illustrates how accounting for implementation heterogeneity and individual compliance can provide insights beyond standard ITT analyses.

title: Is generative AI really changing public sector work? Evidence from a multi-country survey
summary: Artificial intelligence has the potential to transform how public services are delivered, with important implications for public service productivity. But how widely is the technology actually being used - and is it making any difference? Our survey of 3,362 public sector workers across the UK, the USA, South Africa and the EU finds widespread use of AI in every region. Our findings suggest that this spread is being driven by bottom-up individual adoption rather than top-down institutional adoption. In the EU, for example, 65% of respondents use AI, while only 19% say their organisation has formally adopted it. Most users are positive about its effects, with 79% saying AI has improved their productivity. However, only 29% say it has increased what is expected of them at work, raising questions about how truly transformative the technology is so far. Across regions, South Africa is a clear outlier, with the highest levels of use, organisational adoption, optimism and awareness of guidelines.

title: Drift-invariant kernels for discount curve models
summary: Kernel ridge regression estimates the discount curve as the minimizer of a pricing error plus a penalty given by the norm of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. By the representer theorem, the estimate lies in a finite-dimensional affine space that depends only on the kernel and on the cash flow dates of the instruments. We ask when this space is invariant under the risk-neutral drift of the discount curve, so that the estimated curves can be the states of a continuous-time arbitrage-free model. We show that this holds for every grid of cash flow dates if and only if the kernel is of the form $k(x,y)=\e^{b(x+y)}\big(c\,\e^{axy}+1-c\big)$, apart from kernels whose Hilbert space has dimension at most two. For this kernel the estimated curve is an affine combination of flat discount curves, each corresponding to a constant continuously compounded yield. The drift-invariant subspaces correspond to sub-grids of the cash flow dates, and the discounted coefficients have linear risk-neutral dynamics.

title: A Multivariate Generalized Cox Model for Dependent and Simultaneous Default Times
summary: We propose a framework for dependent default times where each name defaults when an increasing driver crosses an independent unit exponential threshold. As in Gueye and Jeanblanc (2022), the drivers may jump, so defaults may occur at stopping times of the reference filtration, including predictable ones, and a common jump may cause no, one or several simultaneous defaults. For general drivers, we derive the conditional joint survival law by a backward recursion; it is an explicit product of survival functions if and only if, for every set of names, the predictable reduction of the compensator of their first default time is deterministic. If, moreover, defaults avoid predictable stopping times, the law is a fatal shock law with hazards identified from the drivers; predictable default atoms can rule this out. Examples include Lévy subordinators and, with random reductions but explicit laws, Liu's model and shot-noise drivers with memory.
